speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the weak response of Canada to the grave injustice and insult of apartheid in South Africa is certain to cause a crisis within the Commonwealth. Canada has the opportunity now to take the lead by imposing strong economic and diplomatic sanctions against the South African Government. The black nations of the Commonwealth can only feel a sense of dismay at our feeble protests in the face of flagrant disregard for human rights by the oppressive regime of apartheid in South Africa.
Mr. Ramphal, Secretary General of the Commonwealth, has said: "If the Commonwealth is to be true to itself, it has no option but to be in the vanguard of the final push against apartheid". The late Right Hon. John Diefenbaker would have added eloquently to those words by concerted action. Why are we doing so much less?

subsubtopic: WHITE FARM EQUIPMENT COMPANY RECEIVERSHIP-EFFECT ON EMPLOYEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bruce Stanley did not understand what the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion meant when the Minister said he was seeking a private sector solution to the problems at White Farm Equipment in Brantford. However, Mr. Stanley knows now. First, the Government refused to give loan guarantees to the company. That meant White Farm was forced into receivership and Bruce Stanley lost his job. Then the receiver took control of the pension fund as an asset of White Farm. That meant Mr. Stanley lost his pension. For his 14 years of service he was offered $2,000 in cash or an RRSP. He needs the money now, but when he takes the measley two thousand bucks, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) will cut off his unemployment insurance.
Now Bruce Stanley fully understands the Government's private sector solution. It means he lost his job, he lost his
pension, and he lost his unemployment insurance. If anyone on the government benches wants Mr. Stanley's phone number, I would be happy to provide it. I do not know what to say to him.

subsubtopic: ANXIETY OF PEOPLE OF SAGUENAY-LAC SAINT-JEAN REGION CONCERNING NEW PAPER PLANT PROJECT IN MATANE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw your attention to the fact that Saguenay-Lac Saint-Jean residents are anxious concerning the proposed establishment of a new paper plant in Matane.
No, Mr. Speaker, people in my region have nothing against a new project which would create jobs in Matane. Far from it, Mr. Speaker! We in the so-called remote regions know only too well how difficult it is to stay afloat, and how much we have to work to attract new job-creating investments to our regions.
Appreciative though we may be of such job-creating projects, the management and staff of the Abitibi Price Company are increasingly worried.
Are we about to create new jobs in Matane, only to the detriment of other workers in the Saguenay-Lac Saint-Jean region, more particularly in Jonquiere and Alma where Abitibi Price is investing $218 million to upgrade its products?
I do not have the answer, Mr. Speaker, but this is a serious matter. I think it is imperative that my constituents be given the full details about this project before our Government decides to award grants.

subsubtopic: NATIONAL OPTICAL INSTITUTE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF START OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday, June 5, the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was in Sainte-Foy to announce the start of construction on the National Optical Institute.
14604

June 18, 1986
This project was made possible as a result of the Canada-Quebec subsidiary agreement on scientific and technological development.
This world centre for excellence has received a mandate to become self-financing within five years. The institute is a private company, which means that close co-operation with the private sector, government and all parties in the industry is essential to its success.
Thanks to this major project, Quebec City is becoming one of the most important hi-tech centres in Canada, and as a Member from that area, I am very, very proud.
This is one more example of the emphasis placed by our Government on the development of high technology, cooperation with the industry and national reconciliation!

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, next Tuesday the Government of Canada will announce that it will continue the Newfoundland Railway. I welcome the announcement. It is no more than the people of Newfoundland deserve, and no more than this Party did when it was in Government by putting $77 million into the railway. However, that does not absolve the Government of Canada from reaching a comprehensive roads agreement. Newfoundland urgently needs roads to be built-the TransLabrador Highway, a road across the northern peninsula to Roddickton and Englee, a road around Hare Bay, and the Trans-Canada Highway itself. The Government of Canada has an obligation to build those roads in Newfoundland and, while I welcome the announcement next Tuesday of the continuation of the Newfoundland Railway, I call upon the Government to make a long-term commitment to building the necessary roads in Newfoundland and Labrador.

subsubtopic: ACQUISITION OF HUMAN RESOURCES IN MINING SECTOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State (Youth) (Mrs. Champagne) recently announced a series of projects that were approved as part of the Innovations Program, one of the components of our Canadian Jobs Strategy.
Mr. Speaker, one of these projects is the human resources acquisition program for the mining industry. It is aimed at setting up a practical training and placement program for graduates in mining technology. Over the next 19 months our Government will be investing nearly one million dollars for Canadian youth.
As a Member of a responsible Government and a Member representing from a mining area, I have complete confidence in the ability and skills of our young people and we will continue to do everything we can to help them become integrated in the labour market in Canada and in Abitibi.

Mr. Speaker, this week on Vancouver Island, in the spirit of protecting the earth and her children from radiation and nuclear war, people from Campbell River in the north and Victoria in the south will walk toward Nanoose to protest the Canadian Forces maritime experimental test range. To the best of our knowledge the Government has not yet signed the agreement allowing for the continued use of the Base by the U.S. Navy. People fear that the Americans may be pushing for a further expansion of the Base as they did successfully in 1967 when the present agreement was signed.
In the meantime, while our Government continues to be very secretive about negotiations with the Americans, U.S. submarines, armed with nuclear weapons, continue to use the Base at an accelerating rate. This Base does not serve Canadian interests and is a continuing threat to world peace. It must be converted to peaceful use.

subsubtopic: POSITION OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY ON TRADE NEGOTIATIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Monday night the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent) went on national television to talk about the problems Canadians have in trade with the U.S. He spoke of the shakes and shingles issue, of the softwood lumber issue, and the number of import harassments that Canadian businessmen face when they trade with the U.S.
He went on to say that Canadian businesses could not compete with the Americans because they have 260 million in
June 18, 1986

their market-place. That, Sir, is just the point. That is the very market that we want to open up to Canadian businesses. We want our businesses to enjoy the economies of scale that the Americans enjoy. I want to thank the Leader of the New Democratic Party for making the case so clearly in favour of the free trade negotiations which have started.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDING TO MAKE PUBLIC BUILDINGS ACCESSIBLE TO DISABLED PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Jobs Strategy is not only a worth-while training and employment development program, it is also proving to be of major benefit to disabled Canadians.
Under the Job Development Initiative $1.4 million has been allocated to date to help make public and private buildings accessible to disabled persons. These funds have been used for structural modifications and the purchase of special equipment for the disabled.
Job training that benefits the disabled-what an excellent way of not only helping unemployed people gain valuable work experience, but also of providing greater accessibility for the disabled.
That is the kind of combined benefits that the Canadian Jobs Strategy is having for all Canadians from coast to coast.

subsubtopic: PRICE OF FARM FUEL IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to bring to the attention of this House the peculiar situation in which Prince Edward Island farmers find themselves.
Unlike other consumers, farmers are charged two different prices for fuel. When they fill up at a gas station they pay one price, but when they buy in bulk for the farm they pay a higher price. It costs about ten cents a litre more for gas to plough a potato field than it does to fill up for a Sunday drive.
Why should farmers put up with this undeserved discrimination when the fruits of their labour is cheap food for Canadians? That does not make a lot of sense to P.E.I. farmers.
I call upon the Government to instruct Petro-Canada to lower the price of bulk fuel sold at the farm gate. After all, is Petro-Canada not supposed to be working for Canadians? Does that not include our hard pressed farmers?

Mr. Speaker, a task force on insolvency commissioned by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has recently presented the Government with recommendations that have won support from business, labour, creditors, and consumers.
Everybody who has had to work with the current Bankruptcy Act knows that it is sadly out of date and places many hardships on employees and suppliers in particular. Change is long overdue and I hope the Minister will put legislation before the House as soon as possible.
The recommendations in the report that would give adequate and reliable wage protection to employees at little cost should be endorsed by all Members of this House.
Unfortunately the Minister's task force did not recommend any measures to help businessmen who might have supplied inventory to a bankrupt firm. If suppliers are not protected, one bankruptcy might very well push a supplier himself closer to bankruptcy.
I ask the Minister to consider allowing unpaid vendors the right to reclaim goods supplied up to two weeks prior to a bankruptcy or receivership. Small businesses are leading our recovery and we should try to help them in every possible way. Bankruptcy legislation is no exception.

Mr. Speaker, when the tritium recovery plant at Ontario Hydro's Darlington nuclear station is completed in 1987 Canada will begin exporting tritium to the United States and probably other countries possessing nuclear power. The Department of External Affairs and the Atomic Energy Control Board have approved Ontario Hydro's export plans despite the fact that tritium is not included in any non-proliferation treaty between Canada and the U.S. This is despite the fact that over 90 per cent of all tritium goes into making new hydrogen bombs, into refreshing existing bombs, and into neutron bombs. This is also despite the fact that tritium is the U.S. military's number one weapons priority, and the U.S. has the power to seize all available supplies of tritium within its jurisdiction.
At best, the export of Canadian tritium will boost the nuclear arms race by freeing up U.S. stocks of tritium for military purposes, and by lending moral support to the current weapons build-up. At worst, Canada could provide enough strategic material to add hundreds of extra nuclear bombs to the U.S. stockpile. I call on the Government to reverse this misguided and dangerous decision.

June 18, 1986

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Solicitor General of Canada):
subtopic: STATEMENT OF SOLICITOR GENERAL OF CANADA
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY ON CLASSIFICATION OF INFORMATION AND SECURITY CLEARANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to inform the House that the Government has undertaken a major reform of its policies governing classification of information and personnel security screening. The current policies have been criticized from all quarters, and justifiably so. Too much information has been classified and far too many security clearances are being requested by departments. The policy on security classification of individuals is a full three decades old, dating back to 1956. Cabinet Directive 35, which guides the security screening process, dates from 1963.

Mr. Speaker, it's time that the Governement brought its security system into the eighties. We are particularly conscious of the mounting cost of the security clearance program and the growing backlog of requests from departments for clearances based on these old policies. In far too many cases, security clearances are unjustified and unnecessary. Such a system undermines security, instead of ensuing its effectiveness.

I am announcing measures today which will ensure a significant reduction in the demand for security clearances, and require that security clearances undertaken are justifiable, equitable and effective. Our new policy is guided by four basic principles. First, we want to ensure that only Government

June 18, 1986
Statements by Ministers
information in respect of which protection from unauthorized disclosure is essential to the national interest is classified for security purposes, and that this information is effectively protected.

Second, we want to reduce the number of positions in the Government of Canada that require the incumbent to be security screened.

Third, we want to better protect the rights of individuals affected by the Government's administrative security system.

And fourth, we want to upgrade the security of Canada by more effectively managing the resources dedicated to the security screening and information classification and protection programs.

Under the new policy, information will only be security classified if it falls into one of six areas: national defence; international affairs; national security, including hostile and subversive activities and threats to the country's security; confidences of Cabinet; federal-provincial affairs; and selected economic interests of Canada. I want to underline that in no way will this new classification system have any effect whatsoever on a person's right to access under the access and privacy legislation.
To reduce the number of positions which require the incumbent to be security screened, the test will be whether an individual has regular and consistent access to classified information as part of his or her official duties. The level of security clearance will be tied directly to the degree of injury the incumbent or contractor could cause if he disclosed information or material assets classified in the national interest.
Based on the degree of injury there will be three levels of security clearance. I believe the vast majority of classified information can be held in the first level, the lowest level. Much tighter control than is now the case will be exercised on the information placed in secret and top secret categories, therefore reducing the necessity for higher level clearances.

The criteria to be used in rejecting a candidate for a security clearance must be up-dated and made more equitable. Security investigations must also be done in a completely fair and defensible fashion and with the consent of the applicants, ensuring that the rights of any individual subject to security screening are upheld.

Our security screening criteria will be brought fully into line with the provisions of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act. The Government has redefined the rejection criteria so that to be rejected on grounds of disloyality there
must be reasonable grounds to believe that individuals are engaged in or may engage in activities which fall within the definition of a "threat to the security of Canada." Under CD 35 a person could be rejected if considered unreliable, not because he is disloyal. This is no longer supportable. Under the new policy, doubts concerning an individual's reliability must be linked to loyality for the employer to reject a candidate for a security clearance. The employer must have reasonable grounds to believe that a person is unreliable.
I want to emphasize to the House that I will soon issue a formal directive to CSIS governing the provision of security assessments which will give the Service detailed guidelines on how the Government expects the new security policies to be put into action. Under my new directive, CSIS may not conduct any security clearance investigation for a department or agency unless the written consent of the individual is first obtained. I will also direct that CSIS conduct all investigations for security clearance purposes in a manner consistent with this consent by the individual and the principles of natural justice, including obtaining consent for the recording of any interviews. CSIS may interview individuals in order to give them an opportunity to resolve any security concerns which might have arisen in the course of the investigation.

I also reaffirm the Government's commitment to a fair and equitable review procedure for those denied security clearance. Under the CSIS Act, the Deputy Head must notify any person denied a security clearance within ten days and of their right to complain to the Security Intelligence Review Committee.

The CIRC has demonstrated its value as a review mechanism by the careful, thorough and fair manner in which it has investigated and reported upon those cases which have so far come before it, and the way in which it has brought the principles of natural justice into play in those cases.

Mr. Speaker, to direct this new system effectively, the Government has charged Treasury Board with responsibility for the overall management of the new policies. The Treasury Board will assist each department in implementation of the program and monitor compliance with it. CSIS will maintain a central index of all security clearances to assist the Treasury Board and the deparments in the management of the screening program.

The new policies I have announced today are based on two requirements: the need for more responsible management of the Government's security system to improve national security; and the need for a fairer and more equitable treatment of public servants and others who do business with the Government.

The reforms we have before us today are in some respect the culmination of significant reforms initiated earlier in this decade by the previous Liberal Government. For instance, the Canadian Security and Intelligence Service Act, which reformed the security service in this country, gave us a much more precise definition of what, in fact, constitutes a threat to the security of Canada.
This is defined as follows: one, espionage or sabotage that is against Canada or is detrimental to the interests of Canada or activities directed toward or in support of such espionage or sabotage; second, foreign influenced activities within or relating to Canada that are detrimental to the interests of Canada and are clandestine or deceptive or involve a threat to any person; third, activities within or relating to Canada directed toward or in support of the threat or use of acts of serious violence against persons or property for the purpose of achieving a political objective within Canada or a foreign state; and fourth, activites directed toward undermining, by covert unlawful acts, or directed toward or intended ultimately to lead to the destruction or overthrow by violence of the constitutionally established system of government in Canada.
Another piece of Liberal reform legislation which has a significant bearing on these new security policies is the access to information and privacy legislation passed by the Trudeau Government in 1983, and currently undergoing a thorough review by the Committee on Justice and Solicitor General. In fact, the access to information legislation forms the basis of this new policy by adopting the same definition of information subject to security classification.
Under this policy announced by the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) information will be security classified if it falls into one of the following areas: national defence, international affairs, national security, confidences of Cabinet, federal-provincial affairs, and selected economic interests of Canada.
Statements by Ministers
Of course, the major piece of reform legislation implemented by the former Liberal Government was the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The new security policy has had to take the Charter into account in so far as it respects the rights of the people affected. It has had to take into account that Canadians now have freedom of conscience and religion; freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including freedom of the press and other media of communication; freedom of peaceful assembly; and freedom of association. I am informed by officials in the Department of the Solicitor General that they believe this new policy is in accord with the Charter, and with the equality rights committee's report. Certainly we in the Opposition will follow closely the administration of this policy.
As the Solicitor General pointed out, the policy on security classification is almost as old as I am, going back to 1956. Cabinet Directive 35, which governs the security screening process, dates back to 1963. Indeed, the 1956 policy, which will be replaced under these new initiatives, talks about sealing wax to protect secret papers in transit. In an age when high speed coded electronic messages are, in most cases, standard operating procedures, it is clear that the old security policies are just about as antiquated as the Minister of Justice's new pornography legislation relating to the general definition of pornography.
It is clear that the old procedures had simply broken down. The volume of information being classified is staggering, and the number of security clearances for public servants and contract employees with the federal Government was getting completely out of control. In 1982 there were 76,000 security checks conducted on public servants. In the last fiscal year this number was reduced to 69,000. Officials in the Solicitor General's Department have said that these new policies could reduce the number of security clearances in most Departments by about 25 to 30 per cent. In some Departments, I am told, the figures could even be higher. If that is the case, then it is a welcome development.
In terms of cost alone the old policies placed a heavy burden on the federal treasury. I am told that a standard field investigation for an individual security clearance could cost anywhere between $1500 and $4000. With the number of people requiring clearances under the old policies it is evident that not only was it ineffective, it was also costly.
Again, with respect to the reduction in the number of security clearances required, we in the Official Opposition will be watching the numbers carefully in the future to ensure that the new policy is, in fact, having the desired effect.
In conclusion, once again I would like to thank the Solicitor General for providing me with an advanced copy of his policy. We welcome the initiative taken by the Solicitor General. It is the culmination of an effort that began a number of years ago. We all agree that the present system is not adequate and we anxiously await the implementation of this new policy which the Solicitor General has introduced today.

June 18, 1986
Statements by Ministers

subtopic: STATEMENT OF SOLICITOR GENERAL OF CANADA
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY ON CLASSIFICATION OF INFORMATION AND SECURITY CLEARANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first echo the comments of my colleague the Hon.Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) in thanking the Solictor General (Mr. Beatty) for having provided me with an advanced copy of his new policy, as well as a briefing by his officials, which was most helpful.
The whole question of security clearances and the classification of documents is one that has been a matter of serious concern for a number of years. We have waited far too long for these important changes. In 1983 the head of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, Mr. Gordon Fairweather, appearing before a committee of the Senate said, "unnecessary security clearances, unnecessarily high levels of classification, and unnecessary snooping into the lives of individuals are not only wasteful of our resources, are not only morally repugnant, but they are discriminatory".
Those are strong words, and clearly in my view those words are merited by the current policy. What we must look at is the extent to which the new changes announced by the Minister in practice are going to get rid of this very serious attack on civil liberties, which is the basis of current policy in this area.
Cabinet Directive 35, which was dated in 1963, in fact was effectively superseded by the 1984 Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act. There is a mechanism for review of security clearances and so on.
In examining the early decisions of the Security Intelligence Review Committee on denials of security clearance, I must say that those decisions are not encouraging at all. The decision involving Mr. Andre Henrie, for example, or the decision involving Jack Gold, in both of those situations, was really quite disturbing in a free and democratic society.
It is when we examine the fine print of the Minister's proposal that I believe in many respects these proposals are giving the illusion of change. Unfortunately the discretion which is left to Deputy Ministers is so broad that there may be no effective change at all.
What are the definitions that the Minister relies on for the classification of documents? He relies on the definitions which are found in the access to information legislation. The definition sections in the access to information legislation have been criticized by witness after witness appearing before the Justice Committee as being far too sweeping, as, in effect, allowing the Government to hide any information it wants. Those are precisely the same definitions this Minister is using to classify government information. That is no progress at all.
What about the second major element, the definition that is to be used for security clearances? What we find the Minister saying is we will use the definition from the Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act of threats to the security to Canada. Once again, that definition is so broad, so openended that, in effect, those Canadians who are not engaging in any unlawful activity whatsoever could be targetted by it. If, for example, a Canadian sends money to a church group in South Africa which supports the African National Congress that individual
could be targetted under the definition of threats to the security of Canada.
By adopting the sweeping definitions in the access to information legislation, and the wide open definition in the Canadian Security Intelligence Service Bill on threats to the security of Canada, we have seen no effective change at all.

Mr. Speaker, these measures give only the illusion of change. The definitions used by the Government are so vague and allow so much discretion tht there is no real change.

Two groups in particular affected in the past by the security clearance provisions will see no effective relief, or at least there is that possibility. Members of parties in this country that many of us might disagree with, but which are legal parties, are targeted still by this definition. The Communist Party of Canada, which is a legal party in Canada and which is entitled to run candidates, and indeed has elected candidates provincially and federally in the past, would deny a person a security clearance.
With respect to homosexuals, the old policy denied homesex-uals the right to security clearances. I have a letter from the RCMP, Assistance Officer in Charge of Internal Security, who states that homosexuality is a reliability weakness identified in Cabinet Directive No. 35. There is no guarantee that that policy is being changed either, despite the recommendations of the equality rights Committee.
My concern about the announcement of the Minister is that we are really getting the illusion of change. What we are effectively seeing is smoke and mirrors, with no real substantial change at all. In fact, we may be moving backwards, because hidden in the Minister's announcement is a suggestion that much tigher control than is now the case will be exercised on the information being placed in secret and top secret categories. We are moving backward in this area, rather than moving forward with effective whistle-blower legislation, for example.
I am pleased that the Minister has eliminated the secret tape recording of public servants. I commend him for moving quickly on that once I drew it to his attention.

Mr. Speaker, I repeat, there has been no effective change. [English]
The changes are largely illusory and the criticisms which were made by many Canadians, including the head of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, remain well founded. These provisions continue to be discriminatory and excessive.
Finally, I suggest that in view of the fundamental importance of these measures, they should be comprehensively
June 18, 1986

reviewed by the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General soon, hopefully early in the fall.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of State (Finance)) moved:
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-96
speechtext:
June 18, 1986
Time Allocation
That, further to the notice given on Tuesday, June 17, 1986, by the Minister of National Revenue and pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 117 in relation to Bill C-96, An Act to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act, one sitting day shall be allotted to the third reading stage of the said Bill; and
That fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for the consideration of government business on the above-mentioned sitting day, any proceedings then before the House shall be interrupted, if necessary, for the purpose of this Order and, in turn, every question necessary to dispose of the said stage of the said Bill shall be put forthwith and successively, without further debate or amendment.
She said: Mr, Speaker, soon after it came to power, this Government introduced a program for economic renewal, which accompanied the economic and fiscal message of November 1984. In it the government envisaged the possibility of limiting the rate of growth of transfers to the provinces as part of a strategy to correct our fiscla situation and stabilize the state of our finances.
More than a year ago, in May 1985, the federal Government announced its decision to limit the rate of growth of transfers under Established Programs Fianacing. At the time the growth of most other categories of expenditures under federal programs had either been reduced or stopped altogether. Transfers to the provinces could not completely be insulated from the Government's efforts to reduce its deficit.
There were no secrets and no surprises.
Bill C-96 was introduced after extensive and prolonged consultations with provinces which began in November of 1984 and continued through to December of 1985. The subject of transfers was discussed with provincial finance Ministers on at least six separate occasions: November, 1984; January, 1985; May, 1985; September, 1985; November, 1985; and December, 1985. EPF was also discussed at the First Ministers Conference in Halifax in November of 1985.
As a result, the provisions of the Bill reflect these federal-provincial discussions and our desire to achieve deficit reduction in the most balanced and reasonable way possible.
The Bill was drafted in early 1986 and given first reading on February 14, 1986. Second reading began in May, and the Bill was referred to committee. The legislative committee on Bill C-96 heard from 18 groups representing a wide variety of interests: organized labour, academics and students, doctors, nurses and other health practitioners, health consumers, and so forth. The Bill was subsequently reported without amendment.
I testified before the Standing Senate Committee on National Finance in the course of its "pre-study" of Bill C-96.1 tabled an explanatory paper for the information of Senators and Members of Parliament. I also testified before the House legislative committee on Bill C-96. I have responded to opposition questions and made clear the case of the Government.
This Bill has now been debated for 11 days. This Bill has been debated for 37 hours. There have been 125 Hon. Members who have spoken. Hansard will show that the debate is exhausted and the argumentation has become repetitious. Enough is enough.
There is always much talk about the national debt and the need to do something about it. The previous Government talked a lot about deficit reduction. In November of 1981, the Hon. Allan MacEachen, then Minister of Finance, said, "I believe we must reduce our deficit and borrowing requirements substantially". He went on to say, "Some restraint must be applied to our transfers to provinces". This Minister boldly proclaimed: "Now I have set myself the task of cutting back the deficit". As we all know, the deficit was not cut back. Government expenditure grew, and debt charges mounted. That is the situation which compelled the Canadian electorate to defeat the former Government. That is the legacy our Government was elected to rectify. Now we must act. Nothing will be gained by delay or protracted indecision. Indeed, much will be lost.
Public debt charges are growing in size and gaining in momentum. If this situation is not addressed, debt charges will erode our ability to sustain the vital social services Canadians now enjoy. More and more federal revenue will be eaten away by spiralling debt charges, and less and less will be available for vital social services. Ultimately, we can only provide what we can afford.
We have carefully reviewed our resources, and the provinces were involved in that discussion. We are collectively working to reduce our over-all debt load. The provinces are also concerned about the federal deficit and the obstacle it represents to continued economic growth of our entire country. Reducing this obstacle to growth benefits both levels of Government. Provinces now enjoy the benefits of Canada's strong economic performance. Provinces will continue to benefit from lower interest rates, increased employment, rising housing starts, and a growing economy.
This transfer to provinces will grow at rates which can be sustained. EPF transfers will total $90 billion over the next five years. That is $25 billion more than over the last five years. Surely this is ample evidence of the federal commitment to health care and post-secondary education. I urge Hon. Members opposite to join with us in support of a measure which both confirms the high priority given by this Government to these social services and the urgent necessity of confronting the federal deficit.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-96
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say at the outset that I am very astounded that the Government would use Standing Order 117, an order which places time allocation on third reading debate on this most important Bill.
I noticed that the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDou-gall) had a little problem with her voice in speaking, and maybe she needs a doctor. I think this very Bill that we are discussing this afternoon is one that will have a tremendous
June 18, 1986

effect on our health care system, on our doctors, our hospitals and our senior citizens. Every individual in Canada who requires some measure of health care will be affected by the Bill. I am astounded that the Government would use time allocation, a Draconian measure, to silence the voice of the people for further debate on an issue as important as this.
I say that I am astounded that the Government is cutting off debate. The reason I say that is that just yesterday I received a telex by special delivery, as did other Members of Parliament, from 128 of the 147 physicians practising medicine in the Province of Prince Edward Island. I will read the telex into the record today. It is addressed to me and it states:
The following list of P.E.I. physicians hereby petition our Members of Parliament, and Parliament, to give favourable consideration to the recommendations of the Canadian Medical Association related to Bill C-96;
1)	That this legislation be restricted to a short-term basis only-and only if absolutely essential to the future economy of the country:
2)	That the financial disadvantages to the Atlantic provinces be excluded from the provisions of this legislation, i.e. that they continue to receive increasing financial support for health care programs on the basis of the existing, established program-funding formula:
The existing formula, now in place, before the legislation changes it-
3)	That the federal and provincial Governments immediately proceed to negotiate a formal agreement for the future financing of health care in Canada. That agreement should: (a) clearly delineate to the Canadian public the constitutional, fiscal, moral and political responsibilities of both levels of Government to finance health care and (b) provide a level of federal financial support that is inversely related to the fiscal capacity of the provinces or otherwise recognizes and compensates for the fiscal inability of some provinces to provide health services that are reasonably comparableed to those of more affluent provinces.
That telex has the signatures, as I mentioned before, of 128 of the 147 practising physicians in the Province of Prince Edward Island.
The Minister of State for Finance just said, "We have had extensive and long discussions with the provinces and different groups". In other words, she said, I believe, they met six times. Well, what kind of discussions were those? When we find that the Canadian Medical Association, universities and provinces are condemning this legislation, we must wonder what kind of two-way conversation took place. It looks to me as though they went to meet with the provinces and with different organizations, and they said what they are saying by Standing Order 117; "We will talk, we will talk so long, but it will be a oneway conversation".
For the Government and for the Minister to stand in her place today and bring down this sort of a Draconian measure with respect to a Bill as important as this is evidence of the desperate situation in which the Government finds itself.
A couple of my colleagues and I attended some hearings in Atlantic Canada with respect to the issue of EPF. We met with hospital administrators who told us, as I am sure they will tell any other Member of Parliament who takes the time to inquire how this Bill will affect them, that they are already
Time Allocation
overburdened, They are already underfunded in terms of meeting the real needs of health care in their areas.
We also met with student unions, groups of students who are having extreme difficulty obtaining some sort of education in the out-lying areas of this country. They are finding it extremely difficult to do so because they know that if this Bill goes through and passes, as it is, their tuition fees will increase. These people are already in areas of the country in which they are unable to obtain half-decent summer employment. Some of them in my area will not be able to find any jobs at all this year. Where will they obtain the money to go to university? It is just an impossible situation. As a result, the educational system in the country will deteriorate, and once again we will have second-class citizens in different parts of the country. That is not at all what we should be striving for in this great country of ours. There should be universal access in every part of the country to the education system.
A news release put out by doctors in Atlantic Canada spells out quite clearly that some 87 per cent of doctors in that area have petitioned their Members of Parliament not to reduce extended federal funding for health services by over $21 million over the next five years. That is what it will cost in Prince Edward Island alone. It is also pointed out in the news release that in addition to the losses cited for P.E.I., Newfoundland stands to lose $95 million, Nova Scotia stands to lose $145 million, and New Brunswick will lose $117 million. These are the very areas of the country which can least afford it.
The Minister mentioned that the Government was elected on a policy of economic renewal. We now find out what that term means. It means shifting the tax burden from Ottawa to the provinces. If the provinces are to try to keep up with any sort of a national health care system or educational system they will have to increase their taxes. That is just what the Government is trying to do. It is trying to reduce its deficit while increasing the deficit of the provinces. My constitutents tell me that tax is tax, whether they pay it to the federal Government or to the provincial Government. Why should there be this extra tax burden? The Government may be able to show on paper, in a couple of years, that the deficit is decreasing, while the provincial deficits will be increasing as a result of its actions. I feel that the Government is certainly headed in the wrong direction by trying to shift a tax burden of $8 billion over the next five years from the federal Government to the provinces. That is just not the way to go about it.
In the last election campaign we heard a great deal about co-operation, this great new co-operative spirit between the federal Government and the provinces. I guarantee Hon. Members that as a result of this Bill that co-operation will disappear. I cannot see any provincial Premier of any political stripe agreeing to this sort of Bill.
I know my time has almost run out. However, I would like to go on. I would like to be able to expand on some of my arguments as to why this Bill should not go ahead. However, under Standing Order 117 I am not permitted to speak at any

June 18, 1986
Time Allocation
greater length. I believe the Government will receive its just desserts when it goes to the polls the next time around. I tell every Member opposite that this legislation is very severe legislation for any Member of Parliament who is trying to get re-elected, particularly those from Atlantic Canada. We cannot afford this very unjust legislation, this Draconian measure which is being brought forward by the Government.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-96
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not understand the Government's proposal. I think it does not realize the kind of problems this measure will cause for the provinces, both for our education system and our health care system, for young and old. A provincial Government cannot maintain these systems without sufficient funding. I am positive the system will start breaking down in a matter of years. I think the Government fails to realize the problems that will result for most provincial Governments. I am sure that in a few years, the federal Government will have to review this legislation.

As I see it, the problem is that the Government has moved with undue haste, not so much in closing off the debate, although I confess that is a bit of an aggravation, but in its effort to cut back on the expenditures at the federal level. It has done one of two things. First, it has either transferred the responsibility to the provinces or it has decided that the systems, both the post-secondary education system and health care, should be reduced as to their effectiveness and openness.
We in Canada have prided ourselves for years in the educational system that we have been able to provide, both for the young and for those who seek to continue their education as necessity requires throughout their lifetimes. Equally, we have prided ourselves for many years in terms of the accessibility of our health care system. We need only look to the Province of Ontario to see what occurs when there is insufficient funds made available for the provision of necessary services. The strike by the doctors, albeit motivated more by greed than by good judgment, I think, nevertheless reflects a fundamental problem of funding within the health care system.
Over the years I have seen, as have many other Members, Governments moving to close wings and remove beds from hospitals which, frankly speaking, were necessary if the level of health care we had up until a few years ago was to be maintained. What I find most disconcerting is that for reasons yet to be explained the Government has decided to run serious risks with the future of accessible health care-accessible in both senses; that is, from the point of view of geography and from the point of view of finances.
I do not think there are many Members of any age in this House who do not recall the problems of the early 1950s, and prior, when there was limited access to health care other than through private plans. Those Members will recall-and if they do not personally recall they would find out about it through discussion with people who lived during that period and were
parents of young families-the amount of debt that they were encumbered with as a result of requiring extensive health care.
What will happen as a result of these measures, the one affecting health in particular, is that we will return to a time when there will not be the accessibility that we have come to expect. In our judgment, we are doing that unnecessarily and without justification. We are now embarking upon the taking of risks without adequate justification, and I could predict the end result of that. My predictions are not always correct, I admit, but nevertheless, in this case I think it is based on some factual information. I predict this will have serious deteriorating effects on the availability of hospital and medical care for Canadians throughout the country.
We are not talking only about the Province of Ontario but about every province. In fact, some provinces will be hit harder by the cut-backs than others. The fact is that even after 20 or more years we have not yet been able to achieve that system of health care that affords to everyone reasonably accessible health care within some fair and definable geographic area. I know that in some parts of northern British Columbia, in northern Ontario and Quebec, in the Maritimes and in substantially large parts of the Prairies, getting to a hospital is a chore in itself. If one happens to be unfortunate enough to live in a less densely populated area which once had a small cottage-type hospital available, given the propensity of Governments to cut back in recent years the chances are that that hospital has been either cut back or closed. The chances are that that particular service has not been replaced by any adequate means of transportation. How often have we heard of elderly and sick requiring care who cannot be transported at a speed sufficient to arrive at hospital in time to be looked after?
With those things in mind, it causes me and my colleagues great concern when the Government moves to reduce the amount of money available for the health care system. That is exactly what the Government has done.
I spoke the other day about this same Bill and I dwelt at some length on the question of post-secondary education. Having said that, I would like to refer anyone who is interested to that particular speech. However, I want to spend a moment or two right now talking about the problem of health care.
For years we have argued that before any decisions are made about the suitability of the level of funding we must take a look at the health care system as it exists, and we must modernize it and bring it up to date. We must make sure that it does in fact use the latest technologies and that we are not overlapping responsibilities. We must ensure that we are taking full advantage of all of the new methods and are not encumbering doctors with jobs that could be done by other health care practitioners. We should try to understand that there are various levels of health care required for different people. For instance, the aged do not necessarily need to be in old age homes if they are provided in-home care, but they are not. It has been proven over the world that in-home care is
June 18, 1986

cheaper than institutionalization. If we were really looking for a way to cut down on the costs of health care, we would be doing a reasonable and accurate analysis to determine whether we are now using all of the most modern and acceptable techniques across the country. However, we are not doing that.
As I am sure many Hon. Members did, last night I watched on television an account of the events taking place in Ottawa and other parts of the country at emergency care units which are being closed down. Doctors decided that they are not going to work. I am not going to argue with them if they do not want to work. I suppose there is nothing I can do about that. There is nothing worse than to be sick and have a reluctant doctor, I suppose. There is nothing worse than to need an operation and have it done by a fellow with a scalpel in his hand and a bitterness in his heart. Whether we or someone sends them back to work or not, clearly they are not going to do the kind of work they ought to be doing. I think that is fair to say.
I was sickened to learn that emergency rooms decided that they would not provide any care at all. Most emergency units, with or without doctors, ought to be able to provide some level of emergency care for people who are in need. The nurses and interns who were in the emergency units ought to have been able to continue to run the units. There should have been a clear delineation of responsibilities in order to take full advantage of all aspects of the system.
Therefore, I suggest that where the Government is falling down lies in the fact that it is looking at only one thing. It feels that if we squeeze the pot smaller, we will in one way or another improve the system of health care. I suggest that that is wrong. It may well be that we could in fact spend fewer dollars, but I do not know if that is true or not. One thing I do know for sure is that that decision cannot be made until we first decide if the system is adequate in its provision of care. We have not yet made that decision and that is why in essence we find this legislation unacceptable and we find the closure motion inappropriate.

Mr. Speaker, as you know, Bill C-96 has been the subject of 125 speeches in 11 days of debate in the House, which is a lot more than 30 hours of debate altogether.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government believes in post-secondary education. The Conservative Government is aware of the important of medical and health care services in each of the provinces.
However, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government is also aware of the national debt, that Liberal legacy worth more than $200 billion, yes, I said $200 billion, while in 1968, and when the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) was

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel obligated to rise and speak on Bill C-96 this afternoon. As everyone who has paid attention to the debate over the last few days knows, Bill C-96 will have the effect of cutting $8 billion from health and educational services by 1992. We have heard individuals say that there will not be any cuts.
On a more serious note, we have heard a Member on the Government side say that we are wasting the time of Parliament and of Canadians. Nothing could be further from the truth. Today we also have an additional component, namely, for the tenth time in this Parliament the Government, with its absolute majority, has the temerity to cut off debate. The Opposition recognizes that with the numbers in the House we cannot win any vote in the life of this Parliament. We knew that; Canadians knew that. However, what Canadians and the Opposition do not accept is that we are unable to debate the business of the country in this Chamber. That is the greatest irony.
We have a Government with an absolute majority which is afraid to discuss issues and to give the Opposition a chance to articulate the concerns of Canadians from one coast to the other on the two crucial elements which form the basis of Bill C-96. It is a shame that with over 200 Members the Government does not have the courage to listen to what Canadians are saying through their elected Members of Parliament. However, despite what I have said about closure, the Hon. Member said that we were wasting time. I would submit, with all due respect, that the Member reflects how out of sync are the Government and the Conservative Party with the aspirations of average Canadians on the street, whether the street happens to be in Newfoundland or in Victoria, British Columbia. If government Members chose to travel and to meet with individuals in their own constituencies, they would know that this particular piece of legislation cuts across two elements of society-on the one hand, the young vis-a-vis education and, on the other hand, the old vis-a-vis health services. They are two crucial programs.
As an hon. friend said earlier, there is only one taxpayer. There may be three levels of government, but there is only one taxpayer. Whether it comes from the federal, provincial, or municipal coffers, that taxpayer wishes to have the services which are part of the social contract of the individual with the country.
June 18, 1986

When we travel across the country-and it is the same in my constituency of York West-and talk with senior citizens, we find out what issues they are concerned about. To a certain degree they are concerned about the pension issue. However, they are also concerned about the health issue, the standard of health care, the delivery of health care, the affordability of health care, and the accessibility to health care. Those are their concerns and they are our concerns with this Bill. We are not wasting the time of Canadians when discussing the merits of this legislation. The Government may believe that it is okay to cut $8 billion by 1992 from health or education if we debate the issue for 25 hours. We are not saying that 30 or 40 hours of debate will make this any better. However, this is the only forum that the Opposition has to prevail upon the mindset which seems to paralyse the Conservative Government. One hopes that because of this debate the Government will finally see that there is something to be said about the Opposition's position.
When I travel across the country and meet with young Canadians the topic of education always comes up. I attended a youth forum two weeks ago at the University of Toronto with Senator Hebert. Virtually the only thing we talked about was accessibility to education. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Cabinet Ministers talk about Canada moving ahead with new technology in the 21st century they always bring up education. They say that our institutions must provide our young people with the know-how to compete in the international community. They say that young people must have a chance to grow and develop through our university and college system in order to have the tools to work with in the market-place so that our country and their own lot can be improved.
What are we to tell the young people? What is the Government telling the young people by cutting $8 billion from education and health services in eight years? What are the young people to say about the leadership at the national level? Very often we say that young people do not have fire in their belly any more. In the 1960s and 1970s young people did not talk only about youth issues and education. They talked about the issues of the day. They articulted on the type of world they would like to have. They talked about the disparity between rich and poor. They talked about the gap between the "haves" and "have nots". They talked about war and peace.
Yes, there is now a silence among the youth of the country. Is that any wonder when they do not have motivation, when they are not inspired by their Government to move on to greater things? The Government is moving backwards. It tells the people that although it speaks of education they are not getting the dough to improve their opportunities. You cannot do that with either the young people or the old.
With regard to health care, we in Ontario are witnessing what happens when medical doctors begin to pull away from the medical system. We have seen the reaction. Last weekend

the Hospital for Sick Children had a telethon on the CTV network. Why should it be necessary to have a telethon for the Hospital for Sick Children? The York-Finch Hospital in my own constituency has been engaged in a door-to-door campaign to raise funds. Constituents are asking me why they should give to the York-Finch Hospital. It is not that they do not want to give; everyone will find $5 or $10 to give to the York-Finch Hospital or the Hospital for Sick Children. The point is that they assumed that part of the tax moneys they have to pay each year goes toward health care, toward acquiring new equipment for the York-Finch Hospital and toward building the new wing at the Hospital for Sick Children.
The hospitals are forced to campaign to raise more funds. They are forced to ask Canadians to give a little extra. They are forced to be the recipients of telethons. They do not like that. They do not like to go door-to-door and almost beg for money in order to be able to provide the health care system which we need and deserve. They, like other Canadians, look to their governments for that leadership. They expect the Government to have the foresight to provide that system.
In 15 years ours will be an aging population. Unless we build the infrastructure now to care for that aging population we will be out of step with the needs of Canadians. If we do not plan now we will not be able to provide the services that will be required in the future. The same applies to education for our young people.
I would like to emphasize once again that Bill C-96 is a betrayal of Canadianism. It is a betrayal of two unnegotiable essential services which Canadians have come to enjoy and expect as part of their citizenship. We have been able to show world leadership in education and, perhaps more important, education. If this Bill is allowed to pass, today will be a sad day for Canada with respect to educational opportunities for our young and a health care system for our aged.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed with a great deal of sadness that we must stand today to deliver a speech on the closure motion which the Government has now introduced on one of the most important Bills that this House will deal with in this session of Parliament. Bill C-96 will cut $5,600 million from the post-secondary education and health care budgets of the country.
This is possibly the best example we have had recently of the tyranny that a huge majority of government Members can provide. The Government has now introduced closure 10 times. It has said that it does not want to hear any more discussion or debate. It does not want to hear Parliamentarians from all sides of the House present the views of their constituents on this issue.
I can understand why the Government would bring in closure today. I can understand why the Government would take the position that it does not want any more discussion. This Government measure is quite Draconian, extremely

June 18, 1986
Time Allocation
regressive and antipeople. If I was introducing such a negative Bill I suspect that I, too, would like to minimize debate.
The Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) stood in her place and said that this Bill went to committee where 18 groups appeared. She omitted something very crucial, that virtually every one of the groups represented at committee spoke against this government initiative. They said that Bill C-96 should not be proceeded with as the Government was attempting. That gives more fuel to the argument that in its present form this Bill is premature. That is why we decided to attempt to hoist this Bill for six months. We wanted to give Members of Parliament a second look at this process and hoped to convince the Government that to cut billions and billions of dollars over the next five years from post-secondary education and health care is wrong.
I must tell you that over the last few weeks, when I returned to my constituency, I made a point of asking people if they knew the Government had a Bill before the House to cut back spending on education, training, research and health care. The typical reaction was sort of a blank stare and gaping mouth. People could not believe the Government of Canada was actually cutting back on health care and post-secondary education. What western industrialized nation other than Canada is cutting back on the money invested in their most important resource, the people of their country?
When you look at the record of that Government it has not always cut back in all areas. It spent $1 billion for the bank bail-out. That is $1,000 million it found over the weekend to help the banks. Then there was the $1 billion tax deal for Dome Petroleum. That did not cause any concern. There was another $1 billion on the Gulf Oil sale. That did not cause any concern. Then of course we get into some other things such as the billions in tax concessions of one sort or another to the corporate sector, for which we get very little in return. By the Government's own admission that is costing billions and billions of dollars in lost taxes. If the Government was interested in cutting back, it could cut back there, to say nothing of the $500,000 capital gains exemption. All those people selling race-horses or jewellery or speculating in land in foreign countries or on foreign stock exchanges do not pay any taxes on the profits from those transactions. We say this is unfair. To give away hundreds of millions of dollars, nay billions, to corporations and wealthy individuals and then say we can no longer afford to invest as we have in health care and post-secondary education is wrong. It is for those reasons that we in the New Democratic Party, along with representatives of the Liberal Party have said, let us pause at this point and examine this matter.
Members of this House from British Columbia have seen the educational system in that province literally fall apart. You would have to look long and hard to find a single educator or any other person seriously interested in education who would say that the Province of British Columbia has not devastated
its educational system. People with special needs no longer have appropriate teachers or classrooms. Gifted young people no longer get the kind of education which will enable them to develop their skills and talents as they should. People who live in the rural areas of British Columbia do not have access, because of geography or financial circumstances, to proper educational opportunities. In the province from which I come education has been cut to the bone. As a matter of fact, even the bone has been cut into. When I see that as a result of Bill C-96 some $650 million will be cut from what that Province would normally get for post-secondary education and health care, I just shudder. What kind of educational system will we then have in that part of Canada? I suspect a similar case can be made for other parts of the country as well, and we are very, very concerned.
Many witnesses came before the committee and literally begged the government Members to give second thoughts to what they were doing with Bill C-96. Delegations representing various elements of the health care and post-secondary education systems came before the committee and literally cried to government Members to stop proceeding with this Bill. I do not think there was a single representative who said, proceed with the Bill.
Are members of the Conservative Government really representing the views of their constituents? I would be very surprised if there are many Members of the House, and I would certainly like to hear from them, who have gone back to their constituents, explained that the Government is cutting $5.6 billion over the next five years from education and health care, and then heard them saying go for it. That is a great idea. I suspect those of us who have held public meetings on these issues in our constituencies will all say that the reaction has been total and universal; stop proceeding with this Bill. Do not go ahead. The country cannot afford to take this regressive step.
If we feel that cutting back our investment in health care is the way to resolve the challenges and issues facing the country in that area, we are very wrong. While recognizing that rationalization of the system must occur, we must also recognize that there should first be an examination and analysis of the system regarding the allocation of funds before we hack away at the money invested. For that reason we are disappointed that this Bill is even before us, and even more disappointed that the Government has introduced closure so we can no longer have the opportunity to reflect the views of our constituents on this legislation.

They talked about a new era of reconciliation and national consultation. They told the people of Canada that they would listen to their views about legislation, rather than ram it through. Those
June 18, 1986

words ring hollow today. Where was the consultation? Where is the new era of national reconciliation with respect to Bill C-96? Perhaps the Government listened to a limited number of groups and organizations, but every one of them objected to this Bill. If the Government was true to its word, which invariably is not the case, then it would not pass this regressive legislation.
Is it any wonder that after less than two years in Government the Conservative Party has frittered away its mandate and has frittered away its trust with the people of Canada, because they no longer trust the Government or the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney)? The electorate has a right to expect its politicians to fulfil their promises, including their promises not to do certain things. The Government, lead by a Prime Minister who is greatly lacking in credibility, honesty and integrity, has frittered away its mandate. The Conservatives had overwhelming support on September 4, 1984, and shortly thereafter, but it has gone. Every public opinion poll that has been published in the last number of months indicates that the Liberal Party is leading the Conservative Party in popular support. Indeed, in the Province of Quebec the New Democratic Party, of all political parties, is leading the Conservative Party. The Hon. Member who spoke previously stood in her place and said: "Everything is well in the state of Denmark". But everything is not well for the Conservative Party. Is it any wonder, when the Conservatives ti y to ram through legislation like Bill C-96?
Bill C-96 will render our health care and post-secondary educational system third class. In my Province of Ontario there will be $3 billion less in federal transfer payments over the next five years. Imagine the impact of this on health care and post-secondary education in the Province of Ontario. There will be fewer hospital beds, and if we think there is a problem today with the doctors' strike in Ontario and the closure of emergency wards in an increasing number of hospitals, wait until we see what happens when a total of $8 billion is withdrawn from health care and post-secondary education.
We in the Opposition have tried to make the Government understand that this legislation is not only bad, it is wrong. The impact on our economy will be devastating. Rather than listening, the Government has decided to invoke closure. The people of Canada are watching and they understand what is happening with the Conservative Government.
I note that you are about to indicate that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. It is regrettable that we are not given an opportunity to further discuss this important piece of legislation. I would ask for unanimous consent to carry on with my remarks, and I am sure you will find that unanimous consent opposite.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the motion presented by the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) with respect to Bill C-96, which concerns transfers made by the federal Government to the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, if we consider the total time spent on debating this Bill and the number of Members who have had a chance to speak in the course of eleven days of debate, during the 37 hours at least of debate we have had on this Bill, I think there comes a time when a Government that is responsible and has consulted all ten provinces, that has consulted with the Opposition, both Liberals and New Democrats, a Government that is concerned about the country's financial situation and has a concern for social justice and fairness to each of the provinces, there comes indeed a time when that Government must decide to deal with the question once and for all.
That is what the Minister of State (Finance) has done with this motion. It means that enough time has been wasted by the Liberals and the New Democrats on useless verbiage, and that we should now proceed with more important matters, with measures that will stimulate the Canadian economy by means of new legislation and new regulations introduced, not on a partisan basis but for the benefit of all Canadians, fairly and equitably.
Mr. Speaker, when the Hon. Member for York South- Weston (Mr. Nunziata) spoke earlier of a sad day for Canada, a day to remember, because the Conservative Government was cutting transfer payments, when he said this I think he was completely mistaken. Why was he mistaken? I will explain. When the Liberal Party was in power, there were increases of roughly 7 and 8 per cent a year. I don't think mistaken, but if I am, I am sure someone will say so. Seven and eight per cent per year on transfers to the provinces, at a time when inflation hovered between 12 and 15 per cent. That was the situation when the Liberals were in power. We are giving a 5 per cent increase. Less than what the Liberals gave, granted. However, thanks to the sound management principles of the Progressive Conservative Government, the inflaton take is now around 4 to 4.5 per cent.
So in terms of net gain, the provinces are better off with what we are giving them than they were under the Liberals, because even when they were getting a 7 per cent increase, they had to forego the 5 per cent they needed to keep up with inflation. The increase we are giving them is a better deal, because the inflation rate has gone down.
Mr. Speaker, that is what I call responsible government. This is a Government that is serious about its responsibilities, that negotiates with each province and considers which areas should be given priority treatment. We are aware, Mr. Speaker, that post-secondary education is important. We realize, Mr. Speaker, that health problems are a serious

June 18, 1986
Time Allocation
concern. However, Mr. Speaker, we must be realistic. And the fact is that we were left a deficit of $200 billion by the Liberals.
When we were elected on September 4, 1984, Mr. Speaker, it was not to make empty promises, it was not to waste money as the Liberals did during their 20 years in office, but it was to restore economic order. By restoring economic order we are in a better position to be more generous with the provinces, to make sure that they get fair treatment rather than mere promises. They expect concrete measures, Mr. Speaker, and that is what we are now giving them.
It has been said over and over again that 125 Members have spoken to this Bill, that they were able to tell the Government everything they wanted to say, so I would suggest the the Liberals are mistaken when they claim that we do not consult. Mr. Speaker, they are more mistaken still when they say that we did not speak to the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, there were more than six meetings with the provinces on this subject during the past year alone. These meetings involved discussions with every provincial Minister of Finance. I think it is perfectly normal that the Ministers of Finance of each province are not quite satisfied. But if we look at the provinces' individual budgets, we see that they also have to put their finances on a sounder basis. Each province has certain choices it must make. We saw this with the Liberal Peterson Government. We saw it with the Liberal Bourassa Government. They are cutting back too. And these are Liberals. I don't understand why the Federal Liberals keep telling us they would not make cuts, but on the other hand, I do understand because spending was a habit with them. And they tended to ignore who was paying the bill, but in fact, it was the average Canadian taxpayer who was paying, Mr. Speaker, and they are the ones we want to help today. It doesn't make sense to let the federal Liberals say things that in the final instance would penalize Canadians, because where would the extra money they want to spend come from, Mr. Speaker? From the taxpayers' pockets? No, we won't do that. We have rationalized public spending in order to stimulate the Canadian economy.
I can hear the federal Liberals in Quebec saying: You have cut back payments to Quebec, and that is outrageous. I may remind them that in 1985-86, we are going to spend $4,091 billion, and in 1986-87, it will be $4,329 billion. Of course, they don't understand about increases because Liberals don't know how to count. That we have seen. The New Democrats, who believe the Liberals, think they are right, but then, they don't know how to count either. Mr. Speaker, the message we want to get across in the House and to the Canadian people is that we have to give a reasonable increase that takes into consideration two basic factors: the federal Government's ability to pay, which is very important, and that each province receives a fair and equitable part of these federal transfer payments.
Mr. Speaker, when we sit down and establish these two equations, the inevitable result is a fair deal, and we must not
forget that we have to give 5 per cent today, even if it is more than the inflation rate, because we have to live with a situation we inherited from the Liberals. We have no choice. We have to live with it. However, Mr. Speaker, first of all and above all, we want to protect transfer payments to the provinces over the long term. We do not intend to throw money around recklessly and thus jeopardize a transfer program that is so important and so vital to our provinces, especially to Quebec. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I fully support the motion presented by the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall), and I take my hat off to her, because at last we have a Minister of State (Finance) with character and the guts, unlike the Liberals.
