speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very sorry to have to be speaking on such an important subject as Bill C-96 on a motion of closure. This is a very important matter for Canadians concerning the cuts in funding by the federal Government for post-secondary education and health care to the provinces. The reasons we were given for closure by the Minister were very unacceptable. She pointed to the large number-actually, not a terribly large number, but a respectable number shall we say-of witnesses who came before committee, and the committee heard them. Here we have a perfect example of the kind of consultation we are getting from the Conservative Government. Yes, 18 witnesses from 18 organizations were heard, and they all told the Minister that the Bill was unacceptable, that it would cause a great deal of harm to the health care system and to post-secondary education. The Government listened but it did not act. It is not really a question that we need more hours of debate; it is that we need a Government that is prepared to listen to people, to listen to good sense and to listen to good recommendations.
One of the promises the Conservatives gave in Opposition was that they would go back to the 1977 formula for funding. Of course, what we see in Bill C-96 is that they are not going back to the funding in 1977; worse, they are cutting what was promised since then. This is an entirely unacceptable and, indeed, very dangerous proposal they have presented us. They would have us believe that these cuts are necessary for other economic purposes, and they talk very piously about cutting the deficit. The deficit, of course, is not even being cut. It will grow at least by $29 billion this year. They would like to think that if they keep it under the magic Figure of $30 billion they are doing us all a favour. The estimate of $29 billion is probably an underestimate, because the Conservatives have not been very good at estimating interest rates or petroleum prices. We will probably have an even higher deficit than $29 billion.
The Conservatives are not cutting the deficit, so what are they doing? They are continuing spending and, indeed, increasing spending in some other areas dear to their hearts, such as trips for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), on the
June 18, 1986

Prime Minister's Office, the camera crews, and all of these frills. They have not shown any kind of restraint in these areas. We would certainly like to see restraint in those areas as a first priority, instead of cuts in post-secondary education, in the training of our young people and retraining for others so they will have the skills for the new technological age in which we live, and adequate health care. Instead, what are they doing? They are diverting money from these social programs into other areas of expenditure. The option they have is simply to collect more taxes.
The Government is indeed a continuation of the previous Liberal Government that simply provided enormous loopholes to the corporations. If the Government began to close some of these loopholes it would have more money for post-secondary education, for research and for health care. If we look at the scale of these loopholes we find it is quite instructive. Let us look at what is being collected: personal income tax, $37.7 billion; corporate income tax, $11.7 billion; sales and excise taxes, $18.9 billion; and other taxes and revenues up to $13.3 billion. These amount to a total of $81.6 billion.
What the Government does not tell us about is the very substantial number of giveaways. We can only make guesses as to precisely what these are, and by my calculation this raises the figure up to $26 billion for 1986-87, when we include the corporate giveaways which are listed, and of course we do not even have them all. For much of the data that the Department of Finance reports it is stated that the figures are not available. It is not to say that they do not exist, but that they are giveaways, which make these a very conservative estimate. Of course, we also have unpaid deferred corporate taxes. This figure now totals $32 billion. If one collected even the interest on that, that would be in excess of $4 billion. That kind of money is very substantial, yet we have a Government that is not prepared to go after money. Instead, what it is doing is cutting the social programs. If it needs to cut spending why does it not look at some other areas of Government spending?
For example, just to give an outline of the very high expenditure items, Armed Forces and veterans expenses are more than $11 billion; External Affairs, even if we do not count aid and export development, which are not strictly speaking External Affairs, but rather subsidies to the business sector, amount to more than $1 billion-$1.3 billion; for the courts, for police, for regulatory work, for legal work, the amount is $3.26 billion. That is an enormous amount of money going toward building prisons, including a new prison for the riding of the Prime Minister. Money is spent on legal advice; so there are more contract lawyers. Much of this involves paying off political favours. This is an enormous amount of money. If I were looking for restraint I would look to these items rather than to social programs, the training of our young people and the retraining of others to allow them to obtain better jobs.
In the area of tax collection and finance the total is $3.5 billion a year. That is the amount of money it takes simply to
Time Allocation
manage financial affairs, to run a big department and to collect taxes. That is a great deal of money. I am sure that there could be economies there. Other administrative charges amount to over $2 billion a year.
However, instead of looking at these important areas the Government cuts into the social programs. The Government admits that our young people, people coming into the labour force, good scientific training and research and development are part of the engine of growth. Yet it has cut into this engine of growth, an extremely misguided move.
The last Conservative Member who rose to speak on this issue defended the Government. I think it is worth referring to what the Quebec Government's reaction was to these cut-backs in federal transfer payments to that province. Quebec, as well as the other provinces, is very much concerned with the losses it will suffer as a result of the passage of Bill C-96. I would like to quote from a letter written by Premier Robert Bourassa to an NDP representative. He wrote:

I am sure you know that Quebec Finance Minister Gerard-D. Levesque announced during the budget speech that his Government had been forced to impose a corporate surtax. The purpose of this surtax is to offset the Quebec treasury revenue shortage due, first to a $66 million payment which Quebec did not receive under the equalization program, second to the $82 million health and post-secondary education transfer payment reduction. The Government of Quebec has promised it would reconsider this surtax imposed as a result of federal cut-backs if the federal Government lives up to its commitments concerning equalization, withdraws Bill C-96, and begins immediate negotiations with the provinces.

The same could be said for other provinces, in the sense that they have asked for negotiations, as was the case back in 1977 when the change was made. This was a negotiated change. We would certainly like to see a negotiated arrangement with the provinces, one that would be acceptable to them and would meet their needs in the important areas of health care and post-secondary education. Instead, more money is being collected in the years in which these cut-backs in postsecondary education and health care financing will be made. However, the Government is directing that money into the private sector. It is continuing its corporate give-aways while adding to other programs, such as export development, which is basically a bonus to Canadian businesses. Even the SEED Program is a way of steering money away from programs which used to be in the non-profit community support sector. That money is now being steered into the private sector.
I see that my time has expired. I simply want to say in closing that this closure motion is shameful. The provinces need this support. It is an important part of Canada's social structure. We should go on to discussing reasonable arrangements with the provinces in these fields.

June 18, 1986

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to speak to the Bill C-96 debate closure motion. Since April 25 more than 125 Members have had an opportunity to take part in the debate on this very important Bill. Mr. Speaker, had they done so to make interesting observations and make suggestions which might have benefited all Canadians, it would have been excellent. But most of them saw this as a chance to make every kind of accusations against our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), against Ministers, and against Members of the Conservative Party.
Mr. Speaker, since April 25 these Members have done little more than peddle falsehoods. To say that transfer payments to the provinces will be reduced as a result of Bill C-96 is a false statement. There has never been any question of reducing transfer payments.
The Party in office has stated over and over again that the purpose of this measure is to slow down the growth of transfers to the provinces, not to reduce them. As everyone knows- including Opposition Members-$25 billion more will have been paid by 1990.
Mr. Speaker, to try to say and make Canadians believe that these measures will endanger our education system and our health system, that the number of beds in provincial hospitals will be reduced is, in a way, a form of exaggerated demagoguery.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill has nothing whatsoever to do with cutting down the number of hospital beds or reducing health and education services throughout Canada. Quite the contrary, the purpose of this Bill is to protect and continue to help support these services. Because if the number of services increases and the same high quality we have today in Canada is to be maintained, we must ensure that the provinces receive funds from the Canadian Government every year, funds that are to be increased annually in proportion to the rate of inflation.
Of course we all realize that no one can give more than he has or spend more than he earns. And every time we ask Canadian taxpayers for more, Mr. Speaker, the same taxpayers are always paying for these services.
If we were to continue increasing transfers to the provinces in accordance with the policy adopted in 1977, it is clear we would very shortly reach spending levels that would be unacceptable and unrealistic.
Mr. Speaker, in September 1984, Canadians decided to elect a responsible Government, a reasonable Government, a Government that would try to control spending, a Government that would try to control the deficit, a deficit that was leading us to bankruptcy.
Mr. Speaker, if you want us to go on debating this Bill ... it has been discussed for many hours with the same things being said over and over again, at first, second and third reading.
They have been saying the same thing all along. That is why I was very happy to speak to this motion for time allocation.

It is absolutely true, Mr. Speaker. The facts are incontrovertible. I challenge the Hon. Member's veracity on that point. Clearly he is not being straightforward. What he is saying is not in accordance with the facts. There will be $187 million less going to the Province of Newfoundland over the next five years than the Government of Canada had agreed to spend in a formal arrangement agreed to with the provinces.
June 18, 1986

The Government abrogated that agreement unilaterally and that is the reality.
I do not care if we call it cuts or slowdowns or whatever, the fact is that the province that has the least fiscal capacity in Canada is going to receive, in order to deal with the education of its young people, its most prized possession, $187 million less over the next five years. That is the reality and those are the facts. Government Members can say whatever they like about the difference between cutting and slowing growth.
The Hon. Member has said that no one can give more than he has. I agree with that. I also agree with the principle of reducing the deficit but the Party opposite was elected to govern and therefore elected to make choices. It is choosing to reduce the deficit by cutting back on a section of society which, I would suggest, is the most important we have that is young people.
Yes, we do have to reduce the deficit but we have to make choices as to where those cuts will be made. I say that when the day of reckoning comes at the time of the next election the people will be able to choose who were for young people and who were against them. I say in all honesty and with all sincerity that this measure hits directly at young people.
University professors are leaving Canada by the hundreds. Research is at an all-time low. Our system of post-secondary education is not just second-rate now, it is third-rate. At a breakfast meeting this morning attended by government Members we heard from the Canadian Association for Continuing Education. At that meeting it was very clearly stated by the teachers themselves that there is probably not one first-class institution left in Canada. That is the reality.
Yes there is a deficit, and yes we have to cut that deficit. Yes, we have to make choices, but do not choose to fight the deficit on the backs of the very people in Canada to whom we should be giving an opportunity. We can talk all we like about industrial strategy, economic policy and free trade, but if we are not going to give young people an opportunity to take part in the jobs the Government says it will create, where is the justice? Where is the fairness of it?
The Government has now added insult to injury. Not only has it told young people that it will fight the deficit on their backs, it has told the Opposition that we cannot talk about it anymore. The Government has now taken from us the last power we have as an Opposition. We do not have any more power. We are 40 and 30 against 211. The only power we have is to hold Bills up and talk about them. The only power left to us is our voices, and we were put here to use our voices in the first place. That is what Parliament is all about.
The Government is going to bring in this measure, but more than that it is going to stop opposition Members from talking about it. It is going to take away from the Opposition the only power it has left. That is the reality of what is happening today and that is what is shameful. That is how the Government has added insult to injury.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, here we are again with another government Bill and another closure motion designed to reduce the amount of time Hon. Members may speak on a very important piece of legislation. Let me say at the outset, with all due respect to the government House Leader, that this is yet another example of the Government's inability to control the schedule of the House of Commons. This Bill has been before us for quite some time, as have a number of other importance pieces of legislation. In the final days of the sitting of this Session we find that the Government is trying to ram some Bills through. It is regrettable.
Let me deal for a few moments with the ramifications of this Bill. Let me begin by talking about my home Province of Ontario and what we see as being the impact of this legislation that is now being rushed through on the ability of the Province of Ontario to provide for the health care and post-secondary education needs of its many citizens.
Earlier today we heard an argument about whether there would be a cut-back or a reduction in the amount going to the Province of Ontario, or to any of the provinces, or whether it was a slowing of the growth of revenue sharing. An arrangement was made a number of years ago between the provinces and the federal Government which set out some rules. In fact, it was a long-term plan. It provided the provinces and the federal Government with a long-term understanding of how revenues would be transferred from one to the other. It provided provinces with the ability to make long-term plans for the provision of services, such as the reconstruction of universities, and for the provision of moneys for instructional staff and materials, to ensure that future generations received the kind of education which was appropriate and needed.
Let us look at the Province of Ontario. In 1986-87, it will receive $146 million less than it would have under the previous agreement. In 1987-88, it will be $243 million less; in 1988-89, $388 million; in 1989-90, $547 million; and in 1990-91, $722 million, for a total reduction of over $2 billion over that five-

June 18, 1986
Time Allocation
year period in the transfer of funds from federal income tax and corporate taxpayers to the Province of Ontario. In turn, the province will transfer those funds to post-secondary educational facilities and the health care system throughout the province.
By reneging on that agreement, the Government is in step with the previous Government. It is finding ways to shift the burden on to provincial Governments. In turn, partially because of that and partially because of their own philosophy, they will transfer the burden to the local level, whether it be in the form of a reduction in provincial support to municipalities, a reduction in grants to universities and community colleges, or a reduction in the amount of money available for hospitals and medical services. Ultimately it ends up back at the property taxpayer level, one of the most regressive forms of raising money for the public good. That form of raising money is not based upon one's ability to pay but upon the value of one's property and how much that value has inflated over the years, not through anything one has done but because the market-place has set the worth of the property.

speechtext:
June 18, 1986
International Land Boundary
To discuss or negotiate the A-B line from Cape Muzon to Cape Chacon into the Portland Canal would be wrong at law. Such an attempt by the Government, whether it is involved in free trade negotiations or trying to cozy up to the U.S. administration, would be wrong because any negotiation of that would lead to giving up part of Canada's sovereignty. It would give up major anadromous fisheries, particularly sockeye, but other species as well that come down south of Cape Muzon and Cape Chacon and can be intercepted by the U.S. fleet. There is the military question regarding the entrance and exit of U.S. Trident nuclear submarines which the Americans have been advocating. There is the access to gas and oil rights under the Dixon Entrance, as well as the prospects of poly-metallic sulphides which have been discovered under the area.
I hope that Members of the House will address this Bill with a sense of urgency so that it may go to committee where any questions by Members, officials or scholars can be addressed and any required change of wording can take place. The Bill could then return to the House for its final process of debate and be voted on by the House and entrenched in law in the interest not only of this generation of Canadians but all future Canadians.
As I stated earlier, to negotiate the A-B line and consider any such move is treacherous at best and treasonous if there is to be any consideration of moving that boundary in the interest of the United States. I look forward to hearing other Hon. Members support the entrenchment of the A-B line.

speakeroldname: Mr. Chuck Cook (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PRIVATE BILLS   INTERNATIONAL LAND BOUNDARY ACT (CANADA-ALASKA) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, were it only so, I would be the first to support the Bill by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton). However, the Hon. Member has substantially misinterpreted the actual situation.
Bill C-270 purports to recognize and declare that the Canada-Alaska land boundary is the boundary established in 1903 by the Alaska Boundary Tribunal. Indeed, that is a fact. The boundary that divides the lands of Canada and Alaska, in this area, is undoubtedly the boundary established in 1903 by the Alaska Boundary Tribunal. No one would dispute or challenge this, in Canada or in the United States.
So far then, the only criticism that should be levelled against Bill C-270 is that it is redundant and unnecessary. It merely states the obvious. What is wrong with that? The trouble with redundancy is that it can make certainty uncertain at times. A solution without a problem may all too easily create a problem. Of course, the boundary dividing the lands of Canada and Alaska is too well established to be threatened. However, Bill C-270 could only give this boundary a different status than that enjoyed by the rest of Canada's long boundary with the United States. Why should it have a different status? Which is the superior status, and which the inferior? Either way, Bill C-270 could raise troubling questions not only for British Columbia but for all other parts of Canada that share a common land frontier with the United States.
It seems, however, that Bill C-270 is intended to deal with more than the boundary dividing the lands of Canada and Alaska. Clause 2 of the Bill states:
For greater certainty, the Canada-Alaska boundary includes the A-B line running from Cape Muzon to Cape Chacon to the mouth of the Portland Canal, and a line running headland-to-headland from Cape Muzon to Langara Island.
There is some indication here that the Bill is intended to define not only the boundary for the land but also the maritime boundary between Canada and Alaska. Unfortunately, however, this intention has not been translated into clear legislative drafting; quite the contrary. As a result, it risks prejudicing Canada's position, not advancing it.
There is no doubt that the A-B line was indeed established by the 1903 Alaska Boundary Award and that it divides the lands of Alaska and Canada. That is the common view of both Canada and the United States. The United States, however, insists that the A-B line is, strictly speaking, a land boundary only, in the sense of a line for the allocation of land territories alone, and not for the allocation of sea areas under the sovereignty or jurisdiction of either country. Canada, on the other hand, has always taken the position that the A-B line is not only a boundary dividing the land but a maritime boundary as well, and that the waters south of that line are Canadian, together with the seabed below them.
Regrettably, because of its imprecision, Bill C-270 could be seen to adopt something like the U.S. view of this matter instead of the Canadian one. The language of the Bill, given the history of this dispute, requires greater precision if it is to avoid being interpreted in such a way. Clause 2 states that the land boundary includes the A-B line but does not make clear that it divides the sea as well as the land.
There is yet another anomaly at the end of Clause 2, where the boundary is said to include "a line running headland-to-headland from Cape Muzon to Langara Island". Unfortunately, the line from Cape Muzon to Langara Island was never part of any line established by the Alaska Boundary Tribunal in 1903. As a maritime boundary between Canada and the United States, moreover, a line running from Cape Muzon to Langara Island would make no sense from Canada's perspective, because such a boundary would give the United States a far greater sea area than it has ever claimed west of this line. Clearly, Bill C-270 not only tends to confuse the U.S. and Canadian positions but it also mixes apples and oranges, lateral limits and outer limits in the sea. If it is intended to clarify matters, it really has not succeeded very well.
I have no doubt that the Hon. Member sponsoring this Bill had the most laudable intentions in mind when he put it forward. But it would be too easy to say, "Oh well! Why fuss about a few technical drafting problems? Let's deal with what was intended rather than what was said". These so-called "technical drafting problems", however, could have unfortunate consequences for Canada. Certainly, it is possible to correct them; but these problems are symptomatic of other
June 18, 1986

difficulties that arise even if we ignore the language of Bill C-270 and address its intentions instead.
Let us imagine for a moment that the Bill before us did enshrine in clear statutory form the longstanding Canadian position with regard to the A-B line in Dixon Entrance. We would still have to ask ourselves whether such a Bill would truly achieve its objectives, or whether it might harm the very interests it sought to protect. I assume that these objectives and interests would be to secure Canada's maritime sovereignty in Dixon Entrance beyond all doubt or challenge. But can any Bill do this any more than a Bill stating that rainfall of North Dakota is not permitted in Manitoba?
The answer is clear. No domestic law or other unilateral action can of itself resolve a boundary dispute with another sovereign state. International law and practice lay down a few basic guidelines for the settlement of maritime boundary disputes between neighbouring countries. I would bring these to the attention of the Hon. Member for Skeena. These were well stated by the Chamber of the International Court of Justice in its 1984 decision in the Gulf of Maine case as follows:
No maritime delimitation between states with opposite or adjacent coasts may be effected unilaterally by one of those states. Such delimitation must be sought and effected by means of an agreement, following negotiations conducted in good faith and with the genuine intention of achieving a positive result. Where, however, such agreement cannot be achieved, delimitation should be effected by recourse to a third party possessing the necessary competence.
Of course, it can be said that the A-B line in Dixon Entrance is itself the result of a third-party settlement by the Alaska Boundary Tribunal. That, indeed, is Canada's position regarding the status of the A-B line as a maritime boundary. The United States, however, does not accept that position. Successive Canadian Governments have recognized that the only way forward in this matter is either by negotiation or international adjudication. So far, negotiation has been the preferred route, although it has not yet brought about the result we in Canada would like to see. Any Bill enshrining the A-B line as a maritime boundary in Canadian law might well rule out the possibility of a negotiated settlement and virtually force Canada to refer the dispute to third-party proceedings. Is that what the Hon. Member for Skeena wants? Is that what this House wants? International adjudication is a valuable last resort, but one to be entered into by design rather than by mere accident.
Hon. Members will be aware that discussions on the West Coast boundaries were suspended in 1979, pending the conclusion of the Gulf of Maine case. With that case behind us, the United States has suggested that the time may now have come to revert to the other maritime boundaries, at least to see if there may be a basis for some negotiated settlement. The Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) has taken this proposal under advisement and has sought the views of the B.C. Government to assist him in determining where Canada's best interests might lie. And he has made it clear that he will only decide the matter in accordance with Canada's best interests.
International Land Boundary
Whether we negotiate now or later, or whether it is ultimately decided to refer the question to third-party settlement, we must still ask ourselves whether any version of Bill C-270 might advance the Canadian position. I have already indicated that domestic legislation would not solve the problem under international law. But could it have some effect on the United States? Let me ask the question another way. How would Canada react if the U.S. Congress were to adopt a law of its own regarding the maritime boundary in Dixon Entrance? Such a law, we can be sure, would incorporate an equidistance line dividing Dixon Entrance equally between Canada and the United States.
That, of course, is the U.S. position regarding the maritime boundary in Dixon Entrance. So far, the United States has only declared its position in a public notice in the U.S. Federal Register, and has done so on the express condition that such notice is without prejudice to any negotiations with Canada. A law adopted by the U.S. Congress in response to some variation on Bill C-270 might not-

June 18, 1986
International Land Boundary
that we can have a Bill which gives us some certainty. It is stated in a clause of the Bill:
For greater certainty, the Canada-Alaska boundary includes the "A-B line" running from Cape Muzon to Cape Chacon to the mouth of the Portland Canal, and a line running headland-to-headland from Cape Muzon to Langara Island.
As I understand the purpose of the Bill as set out by the Hon. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset, I would like to read into the record a letter which might be helpful in this debate. The letter is addressed to the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) and is from Mr. Edward J. Derwinski, Counselor, Department of State, Washington, D.C., and pertains to this particular matter. The letter reads as follows:
I want to assure you that negotiations on Dixon Entrance are not taking place. They will not begin until your Government informs me that it has consulted with the affected fishermen and is ready to proceed.
I understand that representatives from External Affairs are still dicussing the matter with Canadian fishermen.
As you are aware, since the 1930's, our Governments have made efforts now and again to resolve maritime boundary issues. These talks have included the Dixon Entrance area, where the A-B line drawn by the 1903 arbitral panel is deemed by Canada to be a maritime boundary and by the United States to allocate islands. (The U.S. claims an equidistant line.) In 1976, when Canada and the U.S. each declared 200 mile fishing zones, these differences became more prominent.
George Shultz and Joe Clark have a gentlemen's understanding that they would work together to try to solve some of our longstanding differences, like the Pacific Salmon Treaty and acid rain.
Dixon Entrance falls into this category. For our part, we firmly believe that discussions on Dixon Entrance have to take place after each side fully consults with its fishermen. Whenever the Government of Canada is ready to meet, we are prepared to sit and talk about this.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for North Vancouver-[DOT] Burnaby (Mr. Cook), indicated that negotiation is the best way to resolve this difference and international adjudication is the last resort. The Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) might well respond that Canada cannot be forced into third-party proceedings against its will. Strictly speaking, he would be right since the United States and Canada are under no binding reciprocal obligation to refer their disputes to adjudication. However, if we reject negotiation and refuse adjudication, the result is an impasse. An impasse can lead to incidents
International Land Boundary
and incidents can lead all too easily to confrontation in the disputed area. Each side scrambles to stake out its claim at the expense of the other. I need hardly spell out the implications of such a development in the Dixon Entrance area. Currently there is a modus vivendi in the area that is relatively satisfactory to both sides. To be sure, there have been incidents from time to time, but thanks to a policy of mutual restraint, these have been isolated and have remained manageable.
Any version of Bill C-270 would put this delicate equilibrium at risk with unpredictable implications for fishing patterns and offshore resource exploration in the disputed area. The impact on the halibut fishery could prejudice local interests. What about the implications for the Pacific salmon treaty? Surely the last thing we should contemplate at this stage is to say or do anything that might interfere with a successful implementation of the salmon treaty.
We have other outstanding maritime boundary questions to resolve with the United States: seaward of Dixon Entrance; seaward of Juan de Fuca Strait; in the Beaufort Sea; and both landward and seaward of the boundary fixed by the International Court of Justice in the Gulf of Maine area. In addition, we have boundaries to settle with Denmark in the Lincoln Sea and with France off the coasts of Newfoundland and St-Pierre-et-Miquelon.
I have only spoken of the possible implications of Bill C-270 on Dixon Entrance. I do not wish to address its possible implications on other areas in question at this time. Let me only say that I doubt that they have been given adequate thought in the preparation of Bill C-270. That Bill is flawed not only in its drafting but in its very approach to maritime boundary problems.
We do not need legislation to protect Canada's position in Dixon Entrance. We do not need it to convince ourselves of the rightness of Canada's position there. We do not need it to convince the United States of our own convictions. Finally, we do not need it for the greater certainty that Bill C-270 promises but does not truly deliver.
Other speakers on this and earlier occasions have discussed the historical background to the A-B line, the matter we are discussing today. I would like to update that history with some of the more recent events. Since World War I, various incidents have occurred which tend to support Canada's position regarding the status of the A-B line. For example, in 1924, a United States cruiser seized a Canadian fishing vessel in Clarence Strait seven and one-half miles north of the A-B line and over five miles from the nearest United States shore. The U.S. reportedly justified this seizure on the grounds that the vessel was fishing well north of the international boundary. This incident would appear to suggest that the United States considered the A-B line to be a boundary for both land and sea.
It is also worth noting that until at least 1931, the International Boundary Commissioners concerned with fixing the Alaska boundary did not treat the A-B line differently from

June 18, 1986
International Land Boundary
other sections of the Alaska boundary. In particular, during the 1920s, the American Commissioner tried to persuade his Canadian counterpart to agree to request their Governments to move the boundary line from Cape Muzon to the middle of Dixon Entrance because its position at Cape Muzon was anomalous as it meant that there was no United States territorial sea off Cape Muzon. In the 1940s, there were unsuccessful attempts to settle the issue by negotiation. Efforts to negotiate a settlement were made again in the 1970s, but these efforts too did not succeed.
Throughout the years from the late 1890s to the present, Canada has maintained that the waters of Dixon Entrance are Canadian and Canadian practice since that time has been consistent with that position. In this regard, several more recent Canadian measures are particularly noteworthy.
For example, in 1964 when the fishing activities of Russian and Japanese vessels off Canada's West Coast began to increase, the Canadian Government issued them a warning to stay out of the Dixon Entrance and Hecate Strait. Both Governments heeded the warning and apart from a few minor incursions, their fishing vessels have not entered these waters.
In addition, in 1971 under the authority of the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act, Canada delimited its exclusive fisheries jurisdiction within Dixon Entrance and Hecate Strait by means of the A-B line and a line drawn across the Dixon Entrance from Cape Muzon to Langara Island. This action by Canada was protested by the United States. Nevertheless, Canada's position on the status of Dixon Entrance and Hecate Strait has remained unchanged.
Before closing, I would like to refer briefly to Bill C-104, the Canadian Laws Offshore Application Act, which was introduced in the House on April 11, 1986, by the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Crosbie). That Bill is designed to reinforce Canadian sovereignty by creating a more comprehensive legal regime for Canadian offshore areas. The Act would put an end to uncertainty about the application of Canadian laws in all these areas by extending both federal and provincial laws to the offshore.
Of special significance in the context of today's debate is the fact that the proposed Canadian Laws Offshore Application Act includes a provision in Clause 16 that deals with the question of historic waters. That clause is a consequential amendment to the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act. When read together with the definition of internal waters in the same Act, it will amply confirm, if any confirmation is needed, that our historic waters form part of Canada's internal waters and are therefore subject to Canadian sovereignty in the fullest sense of the term.
The proposed amendment regarding historic waters is linked to Clause 9 of the Bill on the offshore application of Canadian laws. That clause would enable the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to certify any geopgrahic area to
be part of the internal waters or territorial sea of Canada. In other words, the Government has already introduced legislation which removes any necessity, if any could be said to exist, for legislation along the lines intended in Bill C-270. Furthermore, it does so without creating problems of the sort described by other speakers during the debate.
I opened my remarks today with a reference to the long and colourful history of the Dixon Entrance question. All Members of the House will agree that this brief account of that history, and of the state practice in the area generally, supports the view that the A-B line is the boundary for both land and water inside Dixon Entrance. That is Canada's long-standing view, and it is this view that Canada can and must affirm in any negotiations with the United States.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PRIVATE BILLS   INTERNATIONAL LAND BOUNDARY ACT (CANADA-ALASKA) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no mention of the word "fish" or "fisheries" in the contents of Bill C-270. However, in the next few minutes I hope to show that we cannot talk about the Dixon Entrance without some discussion of fisheries, particularly Pacific salmon and Canada-U.S. co-operation regarding this great resource.
Those in the Pacific area of Canada know that there are five species of Pacific salmon. By far they are the most important fish stocks on the Pacific coast in both quantity and value. While they have been known by a variety of names, they are perhaps most frequently referred to as sockeye, chum, pink, coho and Chinook. These five species differ in important respects, including their productivity, dependence upon freshwater habitat, size, behaviour, susceptibility to fishing gear, and other qualities.
Salmon have been used by native Indians for time immemorial, and the fish have supported an industrial fishery for more than a century. Therefore, Bill C-206 raises an important question in that it affects our fisheries. Historically salmon became the region's second export after furs when the Hudson's Bay Company began exporting salmon from Fort Langley on the Fraser River in 1830. The first commercial cannery in British Columbia began operations in 1870. Of course, canneries had expanded throughout the coast by the turn of the century, as had the exploitation of salmon stocks.
Until 1903 any variety other than red salmon-that is sockeye, chinook or coho-was rejected by canners. Those of us who have lived in the western part of Canada for a long time know that it is the red sockeye which is most in demand as far as canned salmon is concerned. However, because of poor salmon runs in 1903, canners began processing the much more prolific pink and chum salmon. The use of this fish increased sharply in 1911 in response to a disappointing catch of Fraser River sockeye and increased demands for canned salmon. Since then, pinks and chums have held an important place in the commercial salmon fishery in British Columbia.
According to recent catch statistics, the current harvest of Pacific salmon breaks down roughly as follows: the commercial sector dominates the catch, taking some 93 per cent of the total; net gear takes almost all the sockeye, pinks, and chums,
June 18, 1986

while troll gear takes most of the coho and Chinooks; the sport fishery takes a significant share of Chinook and coho and little else, and accounts for about 4 per cent to 5 per cent of the total catch; and the Indian fishery accounts for about 2 per cent and is directed primarily at sockeye.
Almost since commercial fishing of Pacific salmon began in earnest in the late 1880s, capture of salmon bound for rivers of one country by fishermen of the other has created controversy between Canada and the United States. The earliest disputes arose over American catches of sockeye salmon bound for our Fraser River in British Columbia. Since then the scope of the controversy gradually widened to include problems of interceptions by Vancouver Island fishermen of coho and Chinook salmon bound for the rivers of Washington and Oregon; by Alaska fishermen of salmon bound for the rivers of British Columbia, the Northwest Territories, and Yukon; and by northern British Columbia Fishermen taking Alaska-bound salmon. I am sure the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) knows about those controversies and the involvement of fishermen from the United States and Canada.
The first bilateral accommodation occurred in respect of the management of the fisheries for sockeye salmon bound for the Fraser River. In the late 1880s, United States and Canadian fishermen began fishing vigorously for sockeye salmon bound for the Fraser River. United States fishing took place on the approaches to the river, in the extensive chain of islands at the northern entrance of Puget Sound, whereas the Canadian fishery was concentrated in the estuary and in the river itself. At that time the Fraser run had a marked four-year period, with runs in the 1893-1897-1901 cycle being much more abundant. In lean years Canadian fishermen viewed them-seleves as being at the mercy of their United States counterparts who had, as it were, first crack at the fish. There were also concerns on the part of Canadian and American authorities regarding possible overfishing. That concern exists today; it is an ongoing concern.
In 1908 Canada and the United States formed an International Fisheries Commission to prepare a system of uniform and common international regulations for protection and preservation of the food fish of each nation. That kind of cooperation has characterized the fisheries every since. For Fraser River sockeye, the Commission agreed to apply a three-week mid-season closure and to institute a 48-hour weekly closed period the remainder of the season. However, the regulations were not enforced, and the Commission soon became defunct.
A major disaster, the Hell's Gate rock slide, changed all that. It all but destroyed the major up river sockeye run in 1913 and forced the Governments to renew their joint consideration of the Fraser River problems. Canada took immediate action to clear the slide, but when the runs of all cycles began to decline after 1917, it became apparent that other measures including limitation of the fisheries would be necessary.
International Land Boundary
Again, negotiations were started. It took until 1929, 16 years after the Hell's Gate slide, for an agreement to be signed. Another eight years elapsed before the agreement came into force, and yet another nine years before the Commission, established under the agreement, could exercise regulatory powers over the fisheries. There was much difficulty in reaching any kind of accord during those years.
In the 1950s increasing fishing pressure on Fraser River pink salmon became a matter of grave concern. As a result, in 1957 a protocol to the Fraser River Sockeye Agreement was negotiated. It placed pink salmon on the southern approaches to the Fraser River under an international regulatory regime similar to that for sockeye.
At about the same time, the net fisheries of both countries began to extend seaward from the traditional inshore fishing areas. Such seaward extensions increased the incidents of interception and posed severe problems of competitive overfishing. In 1957, the two Governments reached an informal understanding wherein each country, on a voluntary basis, established administrative lines-the so-called surf lines- seaward, from which net fishing was prohibited.
Although the negotiations which took place between the early 1900s and 1957 overcame some of the difficulties, new problems continued to emerge. In the 1960s the Americans became increasingly concerned about the growth of the Canadian troll fishery. This fishery operated not only off the coast of British Columbia, but also off the coast of Alaska. On the Canadian side, northern British Columbia fishermen were again deeply concerned about the location of the surf line off Alaska.
These negotiations were eventually completed and a satisfactory arrangement was made. It appears that both sides are now following more closely than ever before the measures to control the fisheries. We feel that the Pacific salmon treaty, which established this co-operation, would be in jeopardy if this Bill were allowed to proceed. We intend to do nothing which might prejudice its smooth and successful implementation. Bill C-270 could all too easily have such an effect.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PRIVATE BILLS   INTERNATIONAL LAND BOUNDARY ACT (CANADA-ALASKA) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in discussing the question of Dixon Entrance, it is important to remember that boundary delimitations are more than a matter of law and that they may have a significant impact on the allocation of both living and non-living resources in the area concerned. In the brief time allotted to me I would like to focus on the non-living resource potential of the area surrounding Dixon Entrance.
First, it should be noted that the subsurface geology of Dixon Entrance has not been studied extensively but certain inshore tests, seismic profiles and extrapolations based on wells drilled in Hecate Strait and on Graham Island have offered some clues to assist us in estimating the prospects for oil and gas in and around the area in dispute. The results of these

June 18, 1986
Parole and Penitentiary Acts
analyses indicate, for example, that the volcanic and sedimentary rocks under Dixon Entrance may be sufficiently thick and deep to permit the generation and entrapment of certain hydrocarbons. In general though, the all-over oil and gas potential in the area is believed to be modest at best.
The infrequency of exploration activity in the area and the generally negative results of such activity appear to confirm the modest estimates regarding the potential for oil and gas in that area. The first federal permits for oil and gas in Dixon Entrance were acquired in August, 1961, by Huskey Oil and Calgary and Edmonton corporations. Following a perfunctory seismic exploration program these lands were subsequently surrendered. In December, 1964, Pan American, now AMOCO, filed on permits north and west of Graham Island including the area of Dixon Entrance north to the A-B line. At the same time, outside the entrance, permits were taken up to an equidistant line with the caveat placed on those submerged land areas impinging directly on the line.
Seismic exploration and onshore geological surveys were also undertaken in the area in 1966. Successes, however, were few and far between as evidenced by the fact that the permits inside and outside the entrance were surrendered in December of 1967.
South of Dixon Entrance in Hecate Strait and Queen Charlotte Sound and within the Queen Charlotte tertiary basin Shell Canada acquired exploration permits for about 3.5 million hectares. The company conducted geological mapping and offshore seismic surveys and drilled eight exploratory wells in the period from 1967 to 1969 with generally negative results. In 1970 Shell entered into a farm-out agreement with Chevron Canada Resources whereby Chevron would earn an interest in the Shell offshore area by conducting seismic surveys and drilling two deep exploratory wells.
Currently, submerged lands held by the petroleum industry for exploration purposes include two blocks in Dixon Entrance, a small block by Union Oil Company of Canada located immediately northeast of Graham Island and the north end of a large block in Hecate Strait held by Shell Canada Resources and operated by Chevron Canada Resources under the terms of the farm-out agreement to which I have already referred.
The United States has also indicated some tentative interest in the oil and gas potential of the area. Indeed, in 1984 the United States took the first steps toward calling for bids for offshore leases which would have included an area claimed by Canada outside Dixon Entrance. This action prompted a Canadian protest. Subsequently Canada was informed by the United States that the proposed offers of lease sales had been withdrawn due to lack of interest by the petroleum industry.
Notwithstanding Canadian holdings and some American interest in the area, little new has been learned about the resource base in the area since the late 1960s. This is due in large part to a moratorium on exploration and oil tanker traffic in the area which was imposed in 1972 by the federal Government. This moratorium was intended to prevent crude
oil tankers travelling through Dixon Entrance, Hecate Strait and Queen Charlotte Sound enroute from the Trans-Alaska Pipeline terminal as Valdez, Alaska. Subsequently a federal Order in Council indefinitely relieved existing offshore exploration permit holders from their obligations to conduct exploratory drilling in these waters and prohibited any further drilling.
In 1981 the Province of British Columbia declared the area an inland marine zone. At the same time an indefinite moratorium was placed on offshore exploration in Johnstone Strait south of Telegraph Cove and in the Straits of Georgia and Juan de Fuca. These respective moratoria are still in effect.
In June, 1984, the federal and British Columbia Ministers of the Environment appointed a Five-member environmental assessment panel to conduct a public review of the environmental and related socio-economic effects of any renewed program of petroleum exploration off the west coast of Canada north of Vancouver Island. At that time consideration was being given to lifting the moratorium so that exploration programs could be pursued. Accordingly, the west coast offshore exploration environmental assesssment panel was asked to develop recommendations on the terms and conditions under which petroleum exploration could proceed in a safe and environmentally responsible manner.
During the the course of the review the panel gathered information on the environmental and related socio-economic effects of the proposed offshore exploration program and held two series of public fora in November, 1984, and in the latter part of 1985. Chevron Canada and Petro-Canada were designated by the federal and provincial regulatory bodies as proponents of the offshore oil and gas exloration.
All mineral resource interests are relevant to the issue of the boundary in the Dixon Entrance. I fail to see how they are advanced by Bill C-270. I cannot support this Bill.

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Solicitor General of Canada) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-67, an Act to amend the Parole Act and the Penitentiary Act, be read the third time and passed.
June 18, 1986

He said: Mr. Speaker, a year has passed since Bill C-67 was introduced in the House for first reading. The Bill was called for second reading on September 12 of last year. The House of Commons committee studied it, along with Bill C-68, from September to December. Hours of deliberations devoted mostly to Bill C-67 have led to several amendments which, without affecting the important protections it affords to Canadians, respond to criticisms made by committee members and witnesses. When the Bill was reported to the House on January 23, I was confident then, as I am now, that we had legislation which met the interests of the diverse groups involved.
The Senate has created a pre-study committee which has been sitting since the beginning of February. Members of that committee have not only called officials of my Ministry and myself to appear before them on several occasions, they have visited penitentiaries and talked with staff and inmates. As a result of their deliberations I have decided to incorporate into the law the guidelines the Parole Board will follow in determining whether an inmate should be detained.

Mr. Speaker, I have rarely seen a Bill dicussed at such lenght in committee by both Houses. I am glad that we have finally reached third reading stage and I hope that this bill will receive Royal Assent without further delay.

Canadians deserve the measures contained in Bill C-67 which the Government promised in its first Speech from the Throne some two years ago. These measures alone will not solve the crime problems of Canada but they will correct some of the anomalies which threaten the safety of law-abiding citizens. The Bill will allow the National Parole Board to detain up until the last day of their sentence those inmates who, by all professional accounts, are considered likely to commit a crime of violence against another person. Until now the few offenders who met such criteria had to be released automatically by law on mandatory supervision. No one could prevent such releases.
As the law stands today, when the courts sentence you to prison for nine years, you are back out through the front door after six years unless you have committed a serious offence while in prison, such as participating in a riot or knifing someone while you are there, or some other offence. For the vast majority of inmates, earned remission is appropriate and desirable. It is the Government's intention to see it maintained. However, there is also a small minority of violent criminals, sentenced to prison because of violent acts, who have shown no inclination whatsoever to change their ways and become productive members of society. Their very release from prison threatens the safety and, in some cases, the lives of innocent Canadians. It is that handful of cases we are attempting to address with this legislation.
There is something wrong when, as has happened all too often during my tenure as Solicitor General, I receive a
Parole and Penitentiary Acts
telegram from a provincial attorney general begging me to do whatever I can to prevent the release of a dangerous inmate from prison under mandatory supervision; an individual sentenced to prison because he committed a violent offence, has shown no inclination whatsoever toward reforming himself, and who poses a grave threat to society. The only response I can make, however, is that there is nothing we can do beyond informing the police that this individual is going to be released. That is wrong.
I have had to meet with too many victims and too many families of victims to allow this situation to continue indefinitely. I think it is wrong and they think it is wrong that all too often you can have a situation where a violent criminal is sentenced to prison, released after two-thirds of his sentence, is then automatically out the door, can then commit another offence, be back in prison and back out the door all in less time than the initial sentence was for. That mocks the very principle of the rule of law. It destroys respect for the law. It deeply grieves victims and law enforcement officers who see it happen.
What are we talking about in this Bill? We are saying that in a small number of cases out of the 11,000 inmates we have in the federal correctional system, about 100 a year, and it is hard to be entirely certain because the Bill is not yet law, will be affected by these provisions. First of all, we will be dealing with inmates sentenced to prison for one of the violent offences described in the Schedule of the Bill. It would need to have been clear to the Correctional Service of Canada, the professional case management officers, that this individual has shown no sign whatsoever of rehabilitating himself and that his release from prison would pose a grave risk to innocent members of society. What would happen then? The National Parole Board of Canada would take the decision regarding parole. They have the expertise, experience, background and training to take decisions as to whether or not an individual is too risky to release, whether or not he is ready for reintroduction into society, or whether he should be kept behind bars as part of the sentence passed by the courts.
The National Parole Board would have the ability to take the decision as to whether or not that individual would be able to automatically gain release and be returned to the streets. In those cases where the Parole Board said it was clear to them in their professional judgment, with their years of experience, that an individual is not ready for release and the risk to society was too great, they would have the ability to hold him in prison for up to the duration of the sentence prescribed by the courts. We are not asking to hold them beyond that time. We are saying the maximum time would be the time prescribed by the courts when they passed sentence. However, there should be that discretion in a handful of cases where people's lives or safety would be in jeopardy by releasing the inmate.
You can be certain that I consider detention of an inmate beyond his expected release date resulting from earned remission a remedy of last recourse. Consequently, the most

June 18, 1986
Parole and Penitentiary Acts
thorough procedural safeguards possible are afforded the inmate. The Parole Board will make this decision after consideration of criteria set out in the law and the inmate will have all opportunities to know the case against him and present his arguments to the Parole Board.
The Government has taken into consideration the criticism that extended detention may simply postpone the problem. We believe the Correctional Service and the Parole Board can use the extra time to intervene with those few dangerous offenders and attempt to reduce the risk they pose to society. If at any time during this period there is evidence presented to the Parole Board that the individual has mended his ways, that it is possible for us to take this risk responsibly by releasing him into society, the Parole Board has the ability to then let him out. At any time there is a change in the individual's behaviour or approach, at any time it becomes apparent that it is possible to take a chance on his release, this can be done.
Those people who argue that holding a dangerous inmate in prison for the duration of his sentence prescribed by the courts is wrong because he may still be dangerous at the end are making an argument against incarceration period. It is an argument in favour of never sending someone to prison. What we are saying is that in cases where people are not ready for release they should not be released during the period prescribed by the courts. In those cases where an individual is ready for release, let us take that chance, let us gamble on him and attempt to ensure he becomes a productive member of society. However, with dangerous violent criminals, let us stand with innocent Canadians and ensure that their rights are protected.
I want to remind the Members of this House that the more restrictive measures of Bill C-67 are balanced by provisions which accelerate the consideration for parole of those offenders who pose a very low risk of reoffending.
This Bill will require for the first time that the National Parole Board consider at the earliest possible date of eligibility whether an individual should be released on day parole. The effect of this will be that in the case of good risks, of inmates who do not pose a serious threat to society, more of them will be finding their way out of prison earlier. I think that is appropriate. It will also be balanced off so we will be able to better protect innocent Canadians from those people who pose a very grave risk to society.
Having spent most of the past 14 years as a private Member of Parliament and not as a Cabinet Minister, I am sensitive to the need to fully involve Members of the House of Commons and of the Senate, and to accommodate their concerns to the greatest extent possible. For too many years I sat in opposition as an individual private Member of Parliament, and all too often what we saw was the Government ignoring attempts to improve legislation, or to have input into decisions that were taken. It is for that reason the Government waited until yesterday before calling Bill C-67 for report stage. We wanted
to give the Senate committee, whose pre-study was approved by the Senate in December, a chance to express its views before the ability to move amendments in this House of Commons was closed off.
In committee we listened and we amended the Bill to make improvements. I invited the Senate to engage in a pre-study which would ensure that they could have full hearings and have as much input as possible. As a result of their making reports, the House of Commons would be able to consider those reports before the Bill came to report stage in the House. After that point it is not possible for us to make amendments.
We sat literally for months after the House of Commons committee had completed its consideration and reported the Bill to the House. We invited participation from the Senate committee for suggestions in ways in which the Bill could be improved. I gave to them my sincere undertaking that we would listen openly and in good faith, and that where improvements were suggested which did not detract from the principles of the Bill, which would help the Bill to work better and better protect Canadians, that we would make those amendments. There is a time to listen and there is a time to act. We have listened and we have been responsive where reasonable concerns have been raised, but now is the time to pass this Bill. Bill C-67 is supported by the vast majority of law abiding Canadians. I have no doubt about that.

What ordinary Canadians have told me since my appointment as Sollicitor General can be summarized as follows: Canadians want us to find alternatives to imprisonment for offenders who are not dangerous; however, they also want to be protected against dangerous criminals who have shown no interest in their rehabilitation.

One of the issues that remains in contention with some of the Members in this House is whether the National Parole Board should be taking this decision, or whether the courts ultimately should have the power to make a decision, and weighing whether somebody is ready for release. It is the courts that set sentences in the first place. It is the courts that prescribe the sentence when the inmate is first sent to prison, that is the role of the court.
After that time the expertise and experience of the National Parole Board of Canada is brought to bear on the case to ensure that those people who are ready for release from prison are released on a timely basis, and that those people who are simply too dangerous, who have made no effort toward reform, are not released in order to protect innocent members of society.
If there is a mistake in procedure, if there is a violation of an inmate's rights under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms all of that is appealable to the courts. The question that remains is with whom should the power be vested to take a decision? Who has the expertise, the background, which is the more
June 18, 1986

appropriate body to decide whether an inmate has rehabilitated himself and is ready for release or not? Clearly, any of us who weighs that would have to come to the conclusion that it is the National Parole Board of Canada that has that expertise. The Board makes these decisions on a daily basis and should continue to be able to take them.
Taking this power away from, investing it with the courts, would add to delays, would give to the courts a power which they do not seek. It would be to ask a body, which has already played its role in a process at the front end, where it should be, to assume a responsibility throughout the whole process as to whether or not it was appropriate for an inmate to be released at that point.
The purpose of Bill C-67 is limited. It does not seek to change the nature of the sentence by the court. It is focused only on the remainder of the sentence, which is the responsibility of the Solicitor General to administer. It assumes that if a dangerous offender's status were appropriate it would have been so determined at the time of sentencing by the court. That is the time in which the court should have been involved.
That is why I believe that the National Parole Board is clearly the appropriate agency to take this decision. If an individual's rights are violated, under the Charter of Rights that can be appealed to the courts. If there is an error in procedure that can be appealed to the courts. As to the merits of release of an individual, it should more properly be made by the National Parole Board.
There have been too many victims to delay this Bill further. I have heard from their families, they have written to me, and I have had occasion to listen to them in person. There is no more difficult portion of my job as Solicitor General than to have to sit with the families of the victims of violent crime, to have to sit in one case with the families of some young girls who were allegedly assaulted by an inmate who was released under mandatory supervision. In this case he was released a month early because the controls that the National Parole Board has on inmates under mandatory supervision are less than the controls they have on somebody released on parole.
We have the bizarre situation that because an inmate was so dangerous and such a threat to society, in the view of the National Parole Board, the Board was forced to release him a month earlier than they would have released him if he had been less dangerous. That is a travesty, and it is precisely that sort of situation that this Bill is designed to address. There have been too many victims.
We should do what we can as parliamentarians to say that this victimization must stop. I have seen them, I have met with them, I have read their letters, I have heard their voices when they have spoken to me about their experiences. Nobody pretends, least of all me, that this Bill will end for all time violence by released offenders. There is still a date after which offenders are released. We do not attempt to alter the sentence that was passed by the courts. We cannot guarantee that there
Parole and Penitentiary Acts
will not be violence after that date. Nobody can guarantee that.
There is only one guarantee and it is this; that every further day of delay jeopardizes innocent people. When we continue to talk, it is their safety that is at risk. That is why we have to act now. We have debated this Bill, we have studied this Bill, we have amended the Bill where amendments were needed. Now is the time for us to stand with the vast majority of Canadians in saying that we will do everything within our power as parliamentarians to put an end to the senseless violence. Canadians ask no more than that of us and, surely, they have a right to expect nothing less.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, as the Solicitor General spokesman for the Official Opposition, I am pleased to rise this evening to speak with respect to Bill C-67.1 would like to make it absolutely clear at the outset that the Liberal Party supports the general thrust of this legislation. When I spoke at second reading stage on September 12, 1985, I made it clear that the Liberal Party is concerned about the release of violent offenders. I indicated at the time that Bill C-67 is similar to legislation that was introduced by the previous Liberal administration.
We agree that something must be done and that there is a problem with mandatory supervision. We agree that there should be some method by which the violent offenders could be detained until warrant expiry, if necessary, as an ultimate way of ensuring the safety of the public.
Where we disagree in a very fundamental way is with regard to who should make that decision-whether it be the National Parole Board or the courts. I too listened to the groups. 1 also participated fully at committee and listened to all those who appeared there to make representations and submissions of their point of view with respect to this Bill. I have been convinced that that ultimate decision should be made by the court, for a number of reasons that I will indicate during my submissions.
Before doing so, I want to comment briefly on the process. The Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) commented about the process that we have gone through over the last year. He appeared to be laying blame at the door of the Senate for the fact that it has been a year since this legislation was introduced. I believe it is highly unfair of the Solicitor General to lay the blame for the delay at the door of the Senate, when the delay is quite properly the responsibility of the Conservative Government of Canada.
The Bill was introduced last June. It was not brought on for second reading until September, 1985. It was referred to committee where it was given consideration and reported out of committee late last year. We have waited since late last year for the Bill to be brought forward. It was only brought forward

June 18, 1986
Parole and Penitentiary Acts
at report stage yesterday and the Government was intent on rushing the legislation through, knowing full well that the House is scheduled to adjourn at the end of next week.
This is not the only piece of legislation that the Government is trying to muscle through the House in the dying days of this semester. Earlier today, the Government of Canada, for the tenth time in less than two years, introduced closure with respect to Bill C-86, a measure that would cut $8 billion in federal transfer payments to the provincial Govermment over the next five years. There are other pieces of legislation, including the Young Offenders Act which we also dealt with yesterday, which the Government is trying to rush through.
It leads one to wonder whether the Government is doing a disservice to legislation by simply piling it up and trying to rush it through in the last few days of this session. The cynics would suggest that the Government is intentionally backing up important pieces of legislation, knowing that the summer recess is coming and hoping that the Opposition will simply rubber stamp it through.
I want to indicate to the Solicitor General that we in the Opposition do not intend to obstruct the passage of this Bill or, for that matter, any Bill that is of benefit to Canada and will make our society a better place. We do, however, regret very much the method by which the Government has proceeded over the course of the last two years in dealing with legislation. It has told us at the outset that legislation is important and urgent, and that it is imperative that it be passed by Parliament. We were told that in June, 1985, with regard to this Bill. Yet here we are, a year later, over six months after the committee has dealt with it, and the Government brings the Bill forward.
If it was so important and urgent, why did the Solicitor General wait so long before bringing this Bill forward? The Solicitor General will blame the Senate, but that is a separate body. He had the right as the Solicitor General, as a representative of the Government of Canada, to bring the Bill forward forthwith and pass it through all stages in the House and then have it referred to the Senate. However, as a result of his procrastination, we can be assured that this Bill will not be given speedy passage and will not become law for many months yet. The responsibility belongs to the Solicitor General.
For him to stand in his place today and say that with every passing day the threat to society is heightened and that the public safety is threatened, is an absolute farce. If that were the case, and the Solicitor General were in fact as sincere as he would have us believe and as honest as he would like us to believe, then this legislation would have been brought forward six or seven months ago. Yet he waited until this very late date.
When this legislation was introduced, I indicated that given the fact we were supportive of the Bill in principle we would ensure its speedy passage. Notwithstanding the fact that those statements were made on the public record, the Solicitor General waited. I suspect that one of the reasons why the
Solicitor General waited so long is that there is considerable opposition in his own ranks. We know that during the prestudy of this legislation in the Senate, Conservative Senators supported the reports which have been submitted to the Solicitor General but which he totally disregarded. He knows as well as us that there are Conservative Members of Parliament who object very vigorously and adamantly to certain aspects of the legislation.
I am sure that all Members of the House, and indeed those in the upper chamber, support the principle of this legislation. I include representatives of the New Democratic Party. I am sure that when the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) speaks to this legislation, he will indicate that he is concerned about public safety. I am sure he will say that the NDP would like to see measures that will enhance public safety in whatever way possible. However, as is their prerogative, I suppose the NDP will argue in favour of inmates and inmates' rights.
I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the Hon. Member for Burnaby for having such an interest in the cause of inmates, those incarcerated. It is far too easy for politicians and the general public to be against inmates who are serving time in federal or privincial institutions, and to suggest that they are somehow the complete authors of their own misfortunes and that society has no responsibility. I think we must be grateful that there are those in society like Clare Culhane of the Prisoners Rights Group, who is outspoken and has dedicated her life to the pursuit of fairness and justice for individuals in federal prisons. There are also those in this House who have taken an interest in the plight of prisoners.
As the Solicitor General spokesman for the Liberal Party over the last two years, I have received literally dozens if not hundreds of letters from inmates in prisons throughout Canada who have had grievances with respect to their periods of incarceration. When I was appointed as the Solicitor General spokesman for my Party, my initial reaction was, "Well, inmates do not vote. They are degenerates in society. They have breached some very fundamental laws of society and they are being punished for their crimes". My first reaction was not to bother responding to mail from inmates, or submissions from those who would like to assist those in federal institutions. However, over the course of the last two years, I have come to understand and sympathize, to a certain degree, with the plight of individuals serving prison sentences in Canada. Oh, sure, there are a handful serving time in federal institutions who are absolutely degenerate in every sense of the word. They are but a few. I am speaking of the Clifford Olsons and others who are serving lengthy prison terms for multiple murders, for brutal rapes or brutal assaults against young children or against senior citizens. They are but a handful. The others in federal prisons are serving time because, in a fleeting moment of passion, perhaps in a fit of anger, they have digressed from society's norms and have in some way committed a crime to warrant incarceration.

We know there are great numbers of individuals in federal institutions, and we are speaking of federal inmates here tonight. The Solicitor General indicated that their population numbered 11,000 across Canada. A great number of those do not deserve to be in prison, and even the Solicitor General would agree. Prisons should be a sanction of absolute last resort.
Yesterday, when we were dealing with the report stage of this particular piece of legislation, I indicated that every effort should be made to decrease the prison population in Canada for a number of reasons. We know there are those serving time in federal institutions, sentences of two years or more, who have not committed violent crimes, who have not, in any physical way, harmed society or any individual member of society. They have committed property crimes or fraud, for example, robbery of an unarmed nature. Those are the prisoners I would suggest should not be occupying prison cells, because to deprive a person of liberty should only be the ultimate sanction of the state.
There are those in this House, most of whom sit on the opposite side, who would suggest that the ultimate sanction should be the death penalty. We know that a great number of Canadians believe in the death penalty. I, for one, do not, for moral reasons. I do not believe that the state has a right to end the life of any individual, regardless of how miserable that life might be, regardless of what crime has been committed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Even if they take someone else's life?

That is right, Mr. Speaker. I do not believe anyone, any human being, has the right to take anyone else's life. I do believe, however, that in certain cases, the ultimate sanction should indeed be life imprisonment, but those cases are few and far between.
I think that we in Canada should consider ourselves to be extremely fortunate because of the safe nature of the society in which we live. I, for one, would not trade Canada for any country in the world. This is my country of birth, one of which I am extremely proud. One of the many reasons I am proud to be a Canadian is because of the safety of our streets, of our society because it is, without question, one of the safest countries anywhere in the world.
