was broken. That could only happen in Detroit. It could never happen in our society. It could never happen in Canada. However, my story illustrates the mentality of certain people. It illustrates that, for example, in the United States crime is accepted as a way of life and that it is very upfront and visible. So we are fortunate to be living in Canada.
We have one of the highest incarceration rates in the world, something which I am sure my friend, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), will point out. If because of that we have one of the safest societies in the world, then I suppose one can argue that it is a good result, we should keep incarcerating people if that ensures that we have some degree of safety in society. I do not believe that particular argument has tremendous merit, since there are costs associated with incarcerating people. I indicated earlier that when one considers the 11,000 inmates in federal institutions we cannot consider them all as being in the same category, as being in the same group.
On a number of occasions I have had the opportunity to visit federal prisons. I have had the opportunity to speak to inmates, those who have been convicted of first-degree murder, second-degree murder, rape, armed robbery and crimes dealing with narcotics. There is a whole spectrum of prisoners in our federal prisons. I referred earlier to the sickies, those who are so far gone that, in my view at least, they are not rational, not sane, for the purposes of the criminal law. However, they were deemed to be sane, although I believe, as do a great many people, that it takes an insane mind to commit premeditated murder, to plan, in a very deliberate way, to take the life of another human being. One has to be sick to do that. How can one possibly be a sane human being and decide to rape and kill a young person, a child, as it happens now and again? How could anyone believe that a Clifford Olson, for example, is sane? In my view, one has not to be in full control of one's mental state before one can do that. There are those types of individuals in federal institutions, and there are not many of them, probably a handful, who would do that. Then there are individuals who have been convicted of second-degree murder or manslaughter.
Before I had the opportunity to visit federal prisons I thought, as do a great many people, that those who are serving lengthy prison terms in federal penitentiaries are the worst type of inmates with whom to deal as far as the correctional authorities are concerned. But that is not the case at all, as anyone who has had the opportunity to visit federal prisons will say. I invite my colleagues in the House to take that opportunity some day. I am sure the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) would facilitate a visit for any parliamentarian who would like to visit a federal prison. Those inmates are not the toughest to deal with. After a period of time, those inmates- and I am talking about those who are serving 10, 15 or 20 years-come to recognize and accept the fact that they will be serving a long period of time in an institution. So they have a stake in ensuring a certain level and degree of calm in the penitentiary. They do not want to see riots or trouble. They do not want to see fights. They want their environment to be
clean. They want to ensure that the food is good. They want to ensure that their environment is as pleasant as possible, because they know that they will be there for a long period of time.
You might ask, Mr. Speaker, which offenders are the most difficult to deal with. According to Correctional Services people and inmates to whom I have spoken, the most difficult people to deal with are those inmates who are serving short sentences. In prison jargon, those inmates are called deucers.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, in Canada we have a two-tiered system of incarceration. There is the provincial system and the federal system. All individuals who are sentenced to two years or less serve time in a provincial institution, and all individuals who are sentenced to a period of incarceration of two years or more serve their sentences in federal prisons. That is why we often hear in the media that so and so was sentenced to two years less a day or so and so was sentenced to two years plus a day. That is the method used by courts to ensure that individuals serve their time either in federal prisons or provincial prisons.
I am not dealing here with provincial prisons. In federal prisons, the inmates who cause the most trouble are those who are serving short sentences, the deucers. It is those who are serving sentences of two, three, four or maybe even five years in length. The reason they are the most difficult to deal with is that they do not care if they break the rules of the institution. If an inmate is serving two years plus a day, he does not care whether or not he earns remission.
Let us take as an example an inmate who is serving two years plus a day. He knows that the day he walks into that prison, regardless of what he does, with the exception, of course, of committing another crime, he will earn remission. I believe the formula is that for every month he serves, he gets 15 days off for good behaviour or for participation in prison programs. The result of that is that any inmate is released after serving two- thirds of his or her prison sentence. That is automatic and is called mandatory supervision. It was introduced in 1970. Later on, I would like to review the origins of mandatory supervision and trace its rather unfortunate history over the course of the last 16 years.
Returning to the example of the inmate who is serving two years plus a day, he knows that he is going to get a third taken off the time of his sentence. Right off the bat-

As I was saying, the sentence of that inmate will be automatically reduced by a third. We are dealing with an individual who will, after serving about 18 months or so, be released. He has nothing to lose if he breaks the rules of the prison. He will get himself into fights and he will destroy the facilities.

The point I am trying to make is that there are misconceptions about federal inmates in society. I think we have to be careful, particularly since we are in a position to pass laws here in Parliament, to ensure that we do not base our decisionmaking processes on the myths that exist with regard to inmates, offenders and convicts. For the most part, the subject of crime, inmates and prisons is a very emotional one. It is very easy for us to have our opinions affected by certain myths or misconceptions that exist regarding federal inmates. I would caution my colleagues not to lump together all 11,000 federal inmates and classify them as being the dregs of society and degenerates.
There is a large percentage, though I do not know exactly what it is, of inmates who are one-time offenders and in all likelihood, after being released from prison, will not commit another crime. I am speaking of those who are truly remorseful because of the criminal acts they have committed and truly want to be rehabilitated. There are those who want to rehabilitate and are sorry for what they have done. They are prepared to serve their time and are prepared to readapt to civilian life in a law-abiding fashion.
When considering Bill C-67, I would simply ask that we try to put a human touch on our deliberations and try to understand with whom we are dealing. We are not dealing with monsters. Some of them, yes, can be classified as monsters. However, it is patently unfair to describe all prisoners as monsters. We have to put a human touch to it.

I should like to refer to one of my constituents, but I will not mention her name. A few years ago her husband committed a very serious crime. He was convicted of second degree murder and was sentenced to a very lengthy period of incarceration. This constituent came to my office with her child about a year and a half ago and asked for assistance because of an internal problem her husband had in the institution. I could not help but feel for her when she told me what she does every week. She boards the bus in Toronto to go to Kingston to see her husband. She takes the child along so that she can see her father. This has been going on for years. Her husband will become eligible for parole in a number of years. I have corresponded with him, but I have not yet had the opportunity to speak directly with him. However, through the correspondence one cannot help but feel for him, his wife, and his child. He admits that he did wrong. He knows that he breached a fundamental law of society. He does not resent in any way the fact that he was incarcerated. He believes that serving his time will be his way of paying back, but he also recognizes that he could never repay that lost life.
There are those people inside and outside the House who would argue that he should have been put to death, that there should have been capital punishment for him because he murdered another individual. Having met with his wife and child and having read the correspondence, I cannot help but be impressed with the fact that there is still hope for this family unit, notwithstanding the heart-wrenching turmoil through which the family has gone over the last number of years. They still have hope, and they still have love for one another. They long for the day a number of years off when they will have an opportunity to live their lives together, the day when this individual will have the opportunity to walk out of the gates of the prison as a free man.
I say all this simply to suggest that when we deal with inmates or prisoners, let us not lump them together. Let us try to understand who they are. Let us try to understand that they are human beings.
At this point I should like to interject the fact that our paramount concern is the safety of society. We recognize that such individuals have breached the laws of society and that by so doing they have deprived themselves of their own liberty. The protection of society should be a paramount consideration, but I do not think that society can completely absolve itself of responsibility. Yesterday we dealt with the young offenders Bill. At times we must ask ourselves why a child of 8 years, 10 years, or 12 years of age is a hardened criminal. We must ask ourselves why children of such a tender age are hardened criminals. It is not the fault of the child; it is society's responsibility. We collectively must take that responsibility. As we sit here in the House of Commons, in the plushness which surrounds us, it is all too easy not to accept any responsibility for the ills in society. Each and every one of us sitting in the House of Commons is fortunate to know that we are financially comfortable. The Lord knows that we in the House, at least

As a society we have to take some responsibility for these people. We must try to determine who are these people and why they do what they are doing. For years and years criminologists, sociologists, psychiatrists, and various other experts have tried to understand crime. They have tried to understand why people break the law, why people do not accept some very standard and basic rules. It is more likely that one born to poverty will lead a life of crime than one born with a proverbial gold or silver spoon in his or her mouth.
I should now like to review the legislation before us and try to apply some of my concerns to it. This piece of legislation was introduced over a year ago, and there were reasons for bringing it forward at that time. One reason was that the concept of mandatory supervision introduced by the Liberal administration in 1970 was simply not working as well as it should have been working. At the time of its introduction it was felt that society required some control over offenders after they were released into the community. On listening to the Solicitor General tonight, one would almost think that with the passage of Bill C-67 we could unequivocally guarantee the safety of society. I believe that something very important has escaped the Solicitor General. I do not think he recognizes that some day in the future nearly all inmates will be released.
The Solicitor General used the example of someone who was incarcerated for nine years. He said quite correctly that after six years, because of mandatory supervision and the concept of earned remission, the individual who was sentenced to nine years in prison would be released by operation of law at six years. Let us assume for a moment that there is no such thing as mandatory supervision, that after this individual was sentenced it was up to the Parole Board to decide when that individual might be released.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, an inmate becomes eligible for day parole after serving one-sixth of his or her sentence and becomes eligible for full parole after having served one-third of the sentence. It is important to distinguish clearly between parole and mandatory supervision. There is a sea of difference between the two concepts. For the most part, parole is successful. There are inevitably cases where parolees commit crimes while out on parole, but generally speaking parole is more successful than mandatory supervision. That is because an individual who is sentenced to nine years in prison knows that if he is of good behaviour for three years, if he co-operates with the authorities, participates in prison programs, is remorseful and is able to show the authorities that he will not
create another crime when released and can be integrated into society, he or she will become eligible for full parole after three years. That person is going to do his best to ensure that his record is such that when the Parole Board considers his application for parole he will be considered a prime candidate for parole and released into the community. Of course, there are certain conditions to that parole, such as that he report to a parole officer once a week, sign in with a local police station, continue to reside in a particular community or stay away from alcohol and drugs.
What happens if the person is not granted parole after three years? Let us assume that for some reason the Parole Board decides that the person should not be released into society because he has not displayed conduct becoming a law-abiding citizen and has failed to co-operate with the correctional authorities. He has the opportunity to apply for parole again at a later date.
There are those who, regardless of the number of times they apply for parole, will be denied parole because they have been bad in prison, because of their violent nature or because of their previous criminal record. If the person who is sentenced to nine years in prison is a bad apple, he would know that regardless of what happens, he is able, by operation of law, to earn three years worth of remission. This is the law of Canada. Every inmate is entitled to earn remission while serving time. There is a reason we have the concept of earned remission. It gives the correctional authorities in the prisons of Canada a carrot to dangle to ensure the proper conduct of an inmate. As long as an inmate has hope that his or her sentence might be reduced there is an incentive for that inmate to be of good behaviour.
If the Parole Board decides in its wisdom that this inmate is not going to be released on parole, he is entitled to be released after six years. Under Bill C-67 if this particular inmate falls within certain criteria, the National Parole Board, according to established criteria and procedures, can issue a detention order which is reviewable every year.
Using the example of the nine year sentence, let us assume that this legislation is in place and the Parole Board decides after six years that this inmate is violent and should be kept incarcerated for a further period of one year, and after that decides to keep him in again. After that there is no option. That person may be serving time in a maximum security institution. After the inmate, who has committed a violent crime, has served the nine-year sentence the doors of the prison must be opened.
Imagine the situation, Mr. Speaker. Imagine what is going through the mind of that individual. He committed a crime and was sentenced to prison for nine years. He was refused parole after three years and was possibly turned down on a number of occasions after that. The National Parole Board decided to issue a detention order a first and second time and then the doors are flung open. He goes from maximum security to the streets.

We then have this person who has served nine years of his life in prison. We then open the prison doors because by law he must be released into society. Imagine for a moment this person who has not seen freedom in nine years. He has been kept incarcerated, perhaps in a segregated unit, for nine years. He has to be released into society with no conditions, no supervision, and no ability to exercise any kind of control. I suggest that what the system is doing in that case is nursing a time bomb. Over the nine years this individual has built up resentment, hate and vindictiveness which he might not otherwise have done. You then release him into society. Would it be any wonder if he committed another crime when he was released?
We have to take into consideration the fact that at some point in time, in line with Bill C-67, the inmate has to be released. If the purpose of this legislation is to protect society, we cannot say that we are at least protecting society for another three years in this case. I submit that we might very well be increasing the chance that this inmate will commit another violent crime. If you just release him from maximum security prison into the community, the likelihood of his committing another crime is enhanced. Simple logic will tell you that. I suggest that society would be better off, and there would be less likelihood of this person committing another crime, if there were a method by which some type of control could be exercised over the individual after he was released into society.
Those facts were taken into consideration some 16 years ago. Over the years we have had a number of commissions which have considered the concept of prisons and release and parole and mandatory supervision. We can go back to 1956, 30 years ago, when we had La Commission Fauteux which studied this particular area. In 1969 there was the Ouimet Commission.

This Commission also examined this issue, Mr. Speaker.
Then in 1972 we had the Huguesson Commission that studied this whole area of correctional law. In 1974 we had the Goldenberg Commission. All four commissions recommended that there should be a period of supervision after you release an inmate into society. That is a major factor that this Government should take into consideration.
The Solicitor General might argue that with the case of the nine-year prison term the National Parole Board might simply keep the person incarcerated for two extra years and in the ninth year of his prison term might decide to release him and attach certain conditions of residency, conditions that the individual not consume alcohol, smoke cigarettes or dope, or whatever the case might be.
How is society being served by keeping an individual incarcerated? That is the question we have to ask. The administration preceding this Conservative administration appointed a special committee to look into the whole area of sentencing. It became known as the Canadian Sentencing Commission. It was originally known as the Sinclair Commission named after a judge of the Supreme Court of Ontario. For health reasons he could not complete his task, and Judge Archambault, who was an expert in this area, was appointed to carry on the work of Mr. Justice Sinclair.
The previous Liberal Government felt it important that we look into the whole concept of sentencing. It relates to the legislation very directly because what we are dealing with here is the other end. After a crime has been committed an individual is convicted beyond a reasonable doubt and then he is sentenced. What we are dealing with in Bill C-67 is the release after the inmate has served his or her sentence.
The Canadian Sentencing Commission is going to consider sentencing procedures in Canada. I am sure a lot of Members recall a few weeks ago a special report on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation program on, The Journal, where the disparity in sentencing across Canada was looked into. The show had four or five different cases of varying degrees of manslaughter. It was pointed out that the sentences ranged from no period of incarceration for manslaughter to a lengthy period of incarceration of some 15 or 20 years. The crimes were then compared. There was one crime where a father literally shook his child to death. He was convicted of manslaughter. There was another case where an individual somehow pushed a friend over a balcony after a period of drinking and was given a particular sentence. What the program pointed out in a vivid fashion was that there is a very serious disparity in sentencing in Canada.
Judges have no rules by which to guide themselves when they hand out sentences. The Journal concluded with an interview with the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of

Before being elected to the House of Commons I had the opportunity for a few short years to practise some criminal law. I found in my limited experience that there was, indeed, a problem with the disparity in sentencing. I could sit in a court of law on any given morning and watch a judge banging his gavel in case after case of drunk driving, for example, handing out a particular sentence, and walking into the next courtroom and then handing out a sentence which might be doubled or tripled.
There are those who suggest that there should be a median where the judge would have the flexibility to go 25 per cent one way or the other. As you know, there are very few crimes in Canada that carry a minimum prison sentence. First degree murder has a mandatory prison term of life imprisonment with parole eligibility after 25 years. With the exception of murder and, perhaps, a second offence of drunk driving and importing narcotics, all the other crimes in the Criminal Code of Canada would allow a judge to permit a person who is convicted of a crime, other than those mentioned, to walk away without a period of incarceration. The person could be released with an absolute discharge, a conditional discharge, required to be released on probation, fined or compelled to perform community service work. That is happening more frequently. My experience is with the Province of Ontario where, more often, judges are requiring those convicted of crimes to provide service to the community by working for voluntary organizations or municipal Governments, rather than sending them to prison.
Given the very nature of the sentencing procedure in Canada, the court has considerable discretion in handing out different types of sentences. Even though there is no minimum sentence for a particular crime, there is always a maximum sentence, so that in the worst possible case, the judge has the authority to impose the maximum sentence. Depending on a decreasing scale of seriousness, the person could be given a reduced prison term.
A few years ago it was felt that our sentencing procedure in Canada needed very drastic reform, given the disparity of sentencing. Therefore, the commission was established and, as I understand it, it is required to report in the near future. I am sure that once the commission reports, its recommendations will be far-reaching and the House will no doubt give thorough consideration to the report. It could very well result in some drastic changes in our prisons and further changes to mandatory supervision.

When referring to the parole, time off from prison for good behaviour, and fixed minimum sentence, Mr. Justice Linden said: "These mechanisms unnecessarily distort and complicate the process of sentencing". This suggestion is made by a judge of the Supreme Court of Ontario and President of the Law Reform Commission of Canada. He is a very responsible individual who served with distinction during his tenure as an active member of the judiciary. He is saying, as a judge, that we should abolish these mechanisms because they unnecessarily distort and complicate the process.
What did Mr. Justice Linden mean? Perhaps it is even presumptious of me to try to determine what the justice meant, but I think it is obvious.
Let us again consider the case of the individual who was sentenced to nine years. Let us assume that the jury decides to convict this person beyond a reasonable doubt for a particular crime that this person has committed. The judge has the responsibility to sentence this individual. Let us assume that there is no minimum sentence for the crime that was committed. What factors must the judge take into consideration and what factors is he allowed to take into consideration when sentencing this individual for that particular crime?
Before sentencing the individual, the judge will hear from the Crown prosecutor and defence counsel as to sentence. Unless an agreement has been struck between the Crown prosecutor and defence counsel, the Crown prosecutor will invariably argue for a lengthy period of incarceration. First, he will argue that the crime was violent and that the individual has shown no remorse. He will say that there must be specific deterrents, but more important, general deterrents so that this person could be made an example to society at large. He will then describe the crime and may bring forward witnesses to suggest that this person is of bad character. If the individual has a criminal record, the Crown prosecutor will introduce that as evidence.
On the other hand, defence counsel will try to convince the judge that he or she should hand down the minimum sentence, taking into consideration a number of factors. Of course, defence counsel will emphasize certain factors and de-emphasize others. He might bring forward character witnesses to say what a fine individual this person was, what a fine family person, et cetera. Then he might cite a number of cases involving similar circumstances to support his position that a lenient sentence must be handed down.
After the Crown prosecutor and defence counsel make their submissions, perhaps including various reports, such as medical reports, the judge must then decide what sentence should be handed down for this individual, taking into account these submissions by the two adversaries in our court system. Of course, he will reach back into his experience over the
years. He might have heard a similar case just prior to this one and might use that as a yardstick. He then must make a decision as to the length of the particular sentence. As one can well appreciate, it is not a perfect art, but a sentence must be handed down.
The reason I have spoken at some length about sentencing is that even though the rules of law might state that a judge should not take parole or mandatory supervision into consideration, judges are human beings, and a judge will take into consideration the fact that the person he is about to send to prison will become eligible for parole after a period of time. Obviously, that must be a consideration, even though there might be some rule that states he is not to take into consideration such factors. Not only will a judge- because a judge is a human being-take that fact into consideration, but a judge will also take into consideration the potential for parole. Therefore, when a judge hands down a sentence of nine years, he knows that the person will be out in six years.
Now that we are introducing Bill C-67, can Your Honour see how the Bill will further distort and complicate the process of sentencing? Whereas prior to Bill C-67 a judge would know full well, within a high degree of certainty, that an individual would be released after serving two-thirds of his or her sentence, with Bill C-67, a judge would no longer know that. I would very respectfully submit that that would affect sentencing. That is why I also mention the sentencing commission; because when the sentencing commission comes down with its report, it will no doubt consider parole and mandatory supervision. Your Honour might find that once the Archam-bault Commission hands down its report, this Parliament, once again, will have to consider this particular area.
It might very well be that before this particular Parliament rises to go to the polls once again, we might again be considering this legislation, or legislation that will affect the whole concept of mandatory supervision and parole.
Mr. Justice Linden made these comments in October of 1985 in a paper prepared for a seminar of the Candian Institute for the Administration of Justice. That was several months after this legislation was introduced in the House, in June of 1985, but it was before or during committee consideration.
In the place of the existing system of sentencing Mr. Justice Linden proposes one that would outline typical sentences for normal examples of each criminal offence. What does the justice mean? He means that instead of having a system where one simply stipulates the maximum sentence as found in the Criminal Code of Canada for a particular crime, or the minimum sentence in the odd case when one is dealing with the importation of narcotics or a second offence for drunk driving or for murder, there would be a system which would

outline simply a typical sentence for normal examples of each criminal offence.
There are degrees of violence, or degrees of offences. All murder is not alike. As Your Honour knows, one can commit murder by pulling a trigger and firing a single bullet. One can commit murder by stabbing an individual with a single thrust. Then, again, one can commit murder by blowing up a house in which there is a person, or by blowing up a car in which there is a person. There are various methods by which one can commit murder.
As well, of every crime that is outlined in the Criminal Code, there are those that can be committed in an uglier fashion than others. What the judge is saying is that there should be a "normal" example of each criminal offence. The judge could then distinguish or deviate from that example, depending upon the seriousness of the crime. Mr. Justice Linden says that there is too much disparity in sentencing. In effect, he confirms the report which was aired on CBC's The Journal. He says that judges are told what sentence to impose in the worst case of each crime and that sometimes they are given no choice in imposing a minimum sentence as well.
However, he said, quite correctly, that there are no guidelines for normal cases. I submit that judges who deal with criminal matters in Canada would welcome and appreciate guidelines, some direction, some assistance. This is the reason why, prior to sentencing an individual, a judge will ask the Crown prosecutor and counsel for the accused for submissions in order to gain some assistance to help him or her decide what type of sentence should be handed out. I am certain that most judges would welcome some type of guidelines. The guidelines might very well suggest that the judge take into consideration parole or mandatory supervision. We know that Mr. Justice Linden has advocated the total abolition of that; but there are ways of retaining the present system, I would suggest, while providing guidelines for judges.
Lor instance, Mr. Justice Linden says that hijacking, manslaughter, aggravated robbery and aggravated sexual assault should be among those offences calling for a benchmark sentence of seven years. Mr. Justice Linden explains that the bench-mark sentence would be the typical sentence. He is saying that if someone is convicted of hijacking, manslaughter, aggravated robbery or aggravated sexual assault then the bench-mark sentence would be seven years. He goes on to argue in the paper he presented to the Canadian Insitute for the Administration of Justice that judges should still be free to make an individual sentence lighter or tougher as the circumstances warrant. In his paper he condemns the out-dated sentences provided in the Criminal Code. He applauded the fact that the previous Liberal administration commissioned a royal commission to study the whole concept of sentencing.

The reason I felt it necessary to comment on some of the suggestions made by Mr. Justice Linden is because in my mind it is important to consider when we are dealing with Bill C-67 what is happening when a judge is sentencing an individual. I believe it is important to understand that at the time of sentencing judges take into consideration a number of factors, including the fact that the particular individual would at some point in time be released on mandatory supervision.
As I pointed out a few moments ago, there have been four separate commissions which have studied this whole area, one in 1956, one in 1969, one in 1972 and one in 1974. I would commend to all Members a discussion paper entitled "Mandatory Supervision, a Discussion Paper". It is a report of the Committee on Mandatory Supervision dated March, 1981. It is a very thorough report prepared for the then Solicitor General of Canada, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan). At that time he felt it important to have his Department thoroughly consider the concept of mandatory supervision. The concept was in force for approximately 11 years at that point in time, but there were problems with it. It was felt that it was important to study the area in order for the Department to come up with suggestions.
This particular report looks into the history of mandatory supervision. It points out that the concept of mandatory supervision began in the United States in the 1950s. It points out that in the United States in the 1950s there was a growing belief in the corrective value of release on parole and the control and assistance provided by parole supervision. A national conference on parole convened by the United States Attorney General in 1956 recommended the same conditions and supervision for those being released as a result of remission.
The Canadian delegates to this conference returned to Canada with this recommendation. Some 14 years and several task forces later mandatory supervision was instituted in Canada, in August of 1970. As Hon. Members know several committees and commissions, the National Parole Board and
the police identified the need for a program to provide supervision of all inmates released from prison.
This Bill could very well have the effect of ensuring that there would be no supervision whatsoever, if an individual is kept incarcerated until warrant expiry. I will not refer to this particular report at length. However, I commend it to Members of Parliament, for those who would like a thorough understanding of the history of mandatory supervision in order to understand the problems associated with it and to understand some of the statistics that have been compiled with regard to it. No doubt this report is available from the Department of the Solicitor General.

Before I refer to the report of the Senate committee that pre-studied this legislation, I would like to briefly describe how the legislation would work. As the Solicitor General pointed out, the National Parole Board will be given the opportunity under the legislation to decide in certain cases whether or not an inmate should be released. The National Parole Board first will consider the type of offence the particular inmate was serving.
The Schedule to Bill C-67 outlines what offences should be considered by the National Parole Board. Basically, the legislation would provide an opportunity for the National Parole Board to consider those inmates who are serving time for violent offences. There is a list of some 20 to 25 offences included in the Schedule. The list includes causing injury with intent, the use of a firearm during the commission of an offence, pointing a firearm, prison breach, manslaughter, attempt to commit murder, causing bodily harm with intent, overcoming resistance to the commission of an offence, assault, assault with a weapon or causing bodily harm, aggravated assault, unlawfully causing bodily harm, assaulting peace officer, sexual assault, sexual assault with a weapon, threats to a third party or causing bodily harm, aggravated sexual assault, kidnapping, robbery, arson, setting fire to other substances, setting fire by negligence and conspiracy to commit murder.
If an inmate is serving time for one of those particular offences which are considered to be violent in nature, the National Parole Board has the authority to decide whether or not that particular inmate should be subjected to a detention order which would be in effect for the period of one year. The inmate could have that detention order reviewed after the first year.

There are those people who would argue that that is what they are doing, that is their job, and that they must decide whether or not an inmate should be released on parole. However, there is a difference. An individual released on parole is not entitled by law to be released on parole. An individual who is released on parole is released on certain conditions, and that parole can be revoked if the conditions are not met. On the other hand, mandatory supervision means that an individual is released by the operation of law; by the laws of Canada an individual who is serving a period of incarceration must be released.
There are those people who would argue that the ultimate authority on whether or not an individual should be released, after the date on which he or she becomes entitled to release by virtue of the earned remission provisions of various pieces of legislation, is the court. That final decision, it is argued, should be a decision of the court. The court, at first instance, makes the decision on how long a period of time the individual should be incarcerated. That one provision is the provision which most offends Members of Parliament on this side of the House.

I would like to refer to the twenty-first report of the Senate committee which is dated May 14, 1986. However, before referring to this report, I would like to point out that the Standing Senate Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs is not a study group or task force of the Minister. The Minister would have us in this House and all Canadians believe that the Senate committee was a creature of his Ministry, that somehow he created that committee to consider this legislation. The Senate Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs does not report to the Solicitor General of Canada contrary to what the Solicitor General of Canada might like or believe or want. It is a committee of the Senate and reports to the Senate. Perhaps in the future the Solicitor General could keep that in mind when he refers to this particular committee.
The Standing Committee of the Senate was referred the subject matter of Bill C-67 in advance of it coming before the Senate. Pursuant to the rules of this House and pursuant to Parliamentary tradition it is possible to refer a Bill to the Senate of Canada in order to allow pre-study of it. The Senate was asked to give some sober pre-thought to Bill C-67. I would like to commend the committee for the work it did on Bill C-67. It did not simply read Bill C-67 through and submit a

report. This is not a lengthy piece of legislation. It is comprised of only 19 pages.
The Senate called a great number of witnesses. It listened to the various interest groups involved including the John Howard Society, the Elizabeth Fry Society, correctional officials and a great many other groups and organizations. In addition to listening, the committee considered reports from various groups and organizations. It also went to a number of prisons in order to talk to inmates, wardens, guards, and other people associated with the prison system.
After consideration of Bill C-67, the committee decided to submit an interim report which is the twenty-first report. It is pointed out that the report was not intended to be exhaustive and that the committee would continue its prestudy of the Bill pursuant to the order of reference. In its twenty-first report the Senate committee pointed out four areas of concern. The first area of paramount concern is the area which causes the Liberal Opposition in this House considerable difficulty, that is the issue of judicial determination of detention. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to indicate what the committee had to say with respect to this very important issue.
It said that the first issue has to do with the question of what is the appropriate body to make decisions with respect to the detention of allegedly dangerous inmates beyond the date of their eligibility for release on mandatory supervision. It was the opinion of the committee that the legislation should reflect the principle approved by the Senate when it adopted Bill S-32, on June 6, 1983, in the first session of the thirty-second Parliament, namely that the court rather than the National Parole Board should make decisions respecting the continued incarceration of inmates who would otherwise be eligible for release on mandatory supervision. The committee said that having heard the comments of the Solicitor General with respect to the appropriateness of the board taking on this responsibility it must, with respect, disagree.
While recognizing that the legislation attempts to ensure that inmates are afforded the best procedural safeguards available to administrative tribunals, the committee was still of the view that such decisions affecting, as they do, the liberty of individuals are more appropriately addressed in a judicial rather than administrative forum where affected inmates would have recourse to all the procedural rights and protections available in the criminal courts as well as the distinct right of appeal.
That in a nutshell is what the Senate committee had to say about this very important issue. Senator Earl Hastings is a member of that committee and I would like to publicly thank him for his involvement. For quite a number of years he has had a very keen interest in this area. I know this legislation is very important to him. He has closely monitored the Bill through all stages and on a number of occasions he attended committee to hear testimony.

The House of Commons committee which dealt with Bill C-67 also heard from the John Howard Society. That organization indicated its opposition to the enactment of this or similiar legislation. They submitted a brief and I would like to read from that brief. The Society said it was its intention to suggest amendments which would lessen the problems associated with the Bill as it currently stands. He indicated on a number of occasions that he would but, as you know, the Minister did not attend committee. I suggest that was a betrayal.
I now want to refer to the section of their brief dealing specifically with the issue of judicial determination of detention. They say, in reference to the enormous authority which Bill C-67 vests in the Parole Board, that they believe special safeguards are necessary to ensure the authority is used fairly and judiciously. For that reason, and because the Bill has the effect of lengthening the term of incarceration beyond that which the court anticipated, they recommended that the prisoner designated by the Parole Board to come under the special provisions of this Bill have the right to appeal the decision to a court of law. The appeal court must have authority to reverse the decision of the Parole Board.
What the Society is recommending very strongly is that this discretionary power should rest with the courts. They believe that would make the system a lot fairer. Yet once again the Solicitor General has totally and absolutely disregarded their very persuasive arguments. The Minister will often stand in his place and applaud the work of the Society. He will stand up and congratulate them. He will tell them what wonderful work they are doing. He would not hesitate to try and score some political points by applauding the Society. However, when it gets down to the crunch, he totally disregards them and tells the Society they are out to lunch, he does not agree with what they are saying.
One would hope at the very least that he would have some very persuasive arguments to put forward in order to substantiate his position that the National Parole Board should make the final decision with respect to whether or not a detention order should issue. We have not heard any persuasive arguments. I suppose he has been convinced by the sister-in-law of the Secretary of State for External Affairs that she should be given the authority, along with her colleagues in the National Parole Board. The Solicitor General certainly has not listened to the John Howard Society or the Elizabeth Fry Society, an organization which the Solicitor General would not hesitate to commend for the very fine work it does with regard to female offenders.
The Canadian Association of Elizabeth Fry Societies, which is an association consisting of all the Elizabeth Fry Societies across Canada, made a submission to the Senate Committee
on Legal and Constitutional Affairs with regard to the proposed amendments to the Parole Act, the Peniteniary Act, the Prisons and Reformatories Act and the Criminal Code. This particular submission is dated April 17, 1986. The brief consists of 35 pages.
I wonder whether the Solicitor General has taken the opportunity to read through this very worth-while brief. I would be pleased to refer a copy to him. Given the actions of the Solicitor General, it appears that he has not listened to the Elizabeth Fry Society and has not read this brief. It includes a table of contents at the front of the brief, and perhaps I can refer to it in order to indicate the depth to which the Elizabeth Fry Society went in order to try to persuade the Government of Canada and, the Solicitor General to understand their concerns.
There is an executive summary, a background and then an overview. There is a section of the brief consisting of some five pages entitled "Parole Board Review Prior to Day Parole Eligibility". There are then two pages of recommendations in that particular area. There are another 15 pages devoted to what is entitled "Parole Board Power to Detain". The members of the Elizabeth Fry Society list a number of reasons for their objections.
They object to the selection of offences, the breadth of application, the conviction and sentencing for future behaviour, disclosure of information to the prisoner, the loss of right to earn remission and the value of remission. They object because violence is not predictable. They object by reason of the vagueness of the grounds for determining likelihood for future violence. They object because of the community resource availability, and they object because of the retrospec-tivity of the legislation.
The members of the Elizabeth Fry Society have also devoted a portion of their brief to the issue of one-chance mandatory supervision, which I hope to address in due course. They also address the six-day hold without warrant provision, and then they make some technical comments. The final recommendation is to rescind mandatory supervision.
I want to refer specifically to the portion of the brief which deals with the issue of judicial determination of detention, that paramount issue that the Opposition is concerned about, and the Standing Senate Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs was concerned about. In the executive summary at page (i) of the brief of the Canadian Association of Elizabeth Fry Societies it says:
Bill C-67 would give new powers to the Parole Board to place a detention order on certain prisoners until warrant expiry, or until the order is lifted. These powers will effectively change the role of the Parole Board to a detaining body (which we normally leave to the courts which ensure due process)-
They go on to say the following:
The fact that the Parole Board would be able to use this detaining power in relation to anticipated rather than actual behaviour, based on criteria contained in Regulations, which are themselves broad and which can be amended without Parliamentary scrutiny, make the provision particularly offensive to existing traditions of due process within the Canadian criminal justice system. It is likely

that the new provision will also be found to contravene Section 7 of the Charier of Rights and Freedoms.
An interesting point the Elizabeth Fry Society makes is that they believe, given their experience, that the retroactivity provisions could contravene Section 7 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I wonder whether the Solicitor General has had the foresight to refer the legislation to some constitutional experts to determine whether or not the Bill complies with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The Canadian Association of Elizabeth Fry Societies at page 17 of the brief make some further submissions, specifically with regard to the concept of judicial determination of detention. I would like to quote from page 17 of the brief, which is entitled "Conviction and Sentencing for Future Behaviour". It was pointed out yesterday I believe by the Member for Burnaby quite correctly, that it is impossible to predict with any degree of certainty future behaviour. I suppose there would be those who would argue that you can predict within a certain degree. Given a certain amount of information about a particular individual, you might be able to decide whether or not this person is likely to be violent at some future point in time. It is not a science.

It is important to at least try to predict human behaviour in an attempt to ensure the greatest protection to society.
I agree that there should be some discretion and that there should be some determination as to whether or not the particular violent offender should be detained in custody. The John Howard Society also agrees, according to the brief which they submitted. The Solicitor General agrees and the New Democratic Party agrees, I believe. Let me quote from the brief of the Canadian Association of Elizabeth Fry Societies. They say:
The proposals place the Parole Board in the traditional role of a court, effectively giving it the power of conviction and sentencing, but for behaviour that has not occurred. This cannot be permitted in our justice system. Firstly, CSC's review and that of the Parole Board, based, as they would be, on behaviour that has not yet occurred, offends and sets aside a fundamental principle of justice, that of being held accountable only for behaviour that has occurred or been actively planned. Secondly, the legislated review and hearing process do not provide the safeguards that apply in court (such as right to counsel, strict rules of evidence, right of appeal, etc.) and yet the consequences of the Board review could be extremely serious for the prisoner, resulting in a

The Elizabeth Fry Society made some very important submissions. They were ignored by the Solicitor General. Ele has ignored the Senate committee, the John Howard Society and the Elizabeth Fry Societies.
What about the Correctional Service of Canada? I want to produce a document that refers to the Correctional Service of Canada. The Elizabeth Fry Societies, the John Howard Society, the Senate committee and even the Correctional Service of Canada argue that the court should make the ultimate decision as to whether or not an inmate should be detained until warrant expiry.
They point out that detaining an inmate until the completion of his or her sentence only postpones the problem until warrant expiry. Yet the Solicitor General of Canada cannot seem to understand that at some point an inmate will be released and that an offender who has been deemed to be violent must be released. Even though that offender would have to be released at some point down the road-and we just want to point out the difficulties-we believe that the authority should rest with the courts.
Well, enough on that point. That is the crucial point about which the Opposition is concerned. There are other concerns that were raised by the Senate committee and by the Opposition at the committee level. Briefly, if I might, in the few minutes that are remaining, I would like to-

If I can return to the submissions I was making before I was interrupted by the Conservative Member who just woke up, the second point that was discussed in the twenty-first report of the Standing Senate Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs was the issue of entrenching guidelines in the legislation. The Solicitor General will argue, "Well, we listened to the Senate in that regard because we did in fact entrench some of the guidelines in the legislation". It was not enough. We argued that the guidelines should not be brought forward by way of regulation. We argued, very strenuously, that the guidelines, with regard to the whole concept of detention and the area addressed in Bill C-67, should be part of the legislation itself in order to ensure that the Governor in Council could not amend or change, almost at whim, these regulations that affect the very liberty of an individual.
What did the Senate committee state with regard to this most crucial issue? It stated, and I quote: "The second issue concerns the decision to allow the Governor in Council to make regulations dealing with guidelines with respect to detention orders, the right to assistance at hearings of the board and to such detention orders and the withholding of information from inmates subject to the detention process." Our comments on these matters would be equally applicable if the courts were the decision-makers with respect to detention orders. "The committee considers that the substance of the regulations contemplated to be made pursuant to Section 15.6 of the Parole Act as it would be amended by Bill C-67 should instead form part of the legislation itself." The proposed section would give the Governor in Council authority to make regulations establishing guidelines with respect to the application by the board of subsections 15.3(7) and 15.4()4 and Section 15.5.
"It is clear to the committee that any such guidelines will have an effect upon decisions touching personal rights and liberties and that policy directions as to how these decisions should be reached ought to be given by Parliament itself'.
I would like to underscore that, Mr. Speaker. The Senate further stated: "We hold the similar view with respect to the power to prescribe what information may be communicated to or withheld from an inmate about the evidence which will be presented at a hearing to determine whether that inmate's incarceration should be continued, and with respect to the power to determine whether an inmate is entitled to assistance at a hearing, and the kind and extent of such assistance, as well as the persons or class of persons who may provide it. In this latter regard, we note that the right to counsel was guaranteed under Bill S-32 as proceedings of this nature would have been conducted before a court. In addition, Section 15.6(2)(b) allows the Governor in Council to prescribe the offences, the commission of which will trigger an automatic review. Once again, this is a matter critical to the liberty of incarcerated individuals and, in our view, the offences should be determined by Parliament itself'.

The other very major concern put forth by the Senate committee, that was considered as well by the Elizabeth Fry Society, the John Howard Society and a number of other individuals and organizations, was the issue of limiting one-shot mandatory supervision. I referred to this particular aspect of the Bill some time ago, and I pointed out that there were concerns.
What the Senate basically had to say about this particular aspect of the Bill was that the one-shot mandatory supervision or the denial of the right to earn further remission to certain inmates whose mandatory supervision has been revoked is objectionable to the committee, and I quote from the committee report as follows: "We note that the scope of this amendment was considerably narrowed in the legislative committee of the House of Commons. Only inmates who have been made the subject of formal consideration for detention under proposed Section 15.4 of the Bill but are not detained by order of the board are to lose the right to earn further remission on reincarceration following revocation of their release on mandatory supervision".
The following is most important, Mr. Speaker: "This amendment, however, fails to take into account the criticism

that an inmate may have his release revoked for the contravention of terms and conditions of that release which have nothing to do with his or her perceived or potential dangerousness. Even the narrow class of inmates who would become subject to the one-shot amendment should not lose the right to earn remission by reason of a technical or minor breach of conditions which results in revocation. Your Honour will recall that yesterday, very specifically, the Hon. Member for Burnaby pointed this out and proposed an amendment-which was not agreed to by the Solicitor General-with regard to Clause 4 of the Bill. One might ask, what is Clause 4 all about? If it is revoked, then the individual would not have a further opportunity for mandatory supervision. Why you might ask would one be concerned?
